Bên cạnh bài toán doanh số, Cybertruck liên tục dính bê bối bởi hàng loạt lệnh triệu hồi trên diện rộng, các khiếu nại về chất lượng hoàn thiện, cùng những chỉ trích nặng nề về tiêu chuẩn an toàn. Thậm chí, thiết kế góc cạnh và sắc nhọn của xe khiến nó hoàn toàn không thể vượt qua các bài kiểm tra quy định an toàn va chạm với người đi bộ, biến Cybertruck thành cái tên "bất khả thi" tại thị trường châu Âu và nhiều quốc gia phát triển khác.
Nước cờ tất tay của Elon Musk sang kỷ nguyên AI và Robotaxi
Việc khai tử Cybertruck không đơn thuần là một quyết định cắt giảm dòng sản phẩm kém hiệu quả, mà còn phản ánh một cuộc xoay trục chiến lược toàn diện của Tesla. Hãng xe điện lớn nhất thế giới đang dồn toàn lực chuyển mình thành một công ty trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) và robot, thay vì chỉ đơn thuần là một nhà sản xuất ô tô truyền thống.
Elon Musk xác nhận rằng dây chuyền sản xuất tại nhà máy Gigafactory Texas sẽ được cải tạo và tái định vị hoàn toàn để dọn chỗ cho việc đẩy mạnh sản xuất Cybercab – dòng xe robotaxi tự lái không vô lăng. Sản phẩm được kỳ vọng sẽ là "con gà đẻ trứng vàng" trong tương lai. Wes Morrill, kỹ sư trưởng của dự án Cybertruck, cũng chia sẻ trên mạng xã hội rằng dòng xe này dù khép lại sứ mệnh thương mại vẫn đóng vai trò là một nền tảng phát triển công nghệ mang tính bước ngoặt cũng như là nền tảng cho các thế hệ phương tiện tự lái sau này.
Trên nền tảng X, Elon Musk viết: "Tesla sẽ ngừng sản xuất Cybertruck tại nhà máy Gigafactory Texas vào khoảng giữa năm sau để dành chỗ cho việc sản xuất Cybercab."
Dấu chấm hết cho một vương miện thị phi
Đáp lại một người dùng trên X, Elon Musk gọi Cybertruck là "chiếc xe tốt nhất mà Tesla từng sản xuất", đồng thời ca ngợi "sự kết thúc của một kỷ nguyên".
Quyết định dừng sản xuất Cybertruck vào giữa năm 2027 đánh dấu sự khép lại của một trong những dự án tốn nhiều giấy mực nhất lịch sử ngành xe điện. Từ một biểu tượng phô trương sức mạnh kỹ thuật, Cybertruck cuối cùng phải ngậm ngùi nhường chỗ cho những canh bạc lớn hơn về tự động hóa và AI.
Trong cuộc đua khốc liệt mà biên độ sai lầm được đo bằng hàng tỷ USD, thị trường đã đưa ra phán quyết tàn nhẫn, những thiết kế gây tranh cãi và không mang lại giá trị sử dụng cao cuối cùng sẽ bị đào thải, nhường lại sân khấu cho các giải pháp giao thông tối ưu và thông minh hơn./

articles.title: Giá vàng giảm, có nên rút tiết kiệm 100 triệu đồng mua vàng?
articles.text:
Sau khi theo dõi diễn biến giá vàng trong nước, chị Bích Hạnh (nhân viên văn phòng tại Hà Nội) đang phân vân có nên sử dụng khoản tiền tiết kiệm 100 triệu đồng để mua vàng tích trữ hay không.
Chị Hạnh cho biết, trước đây, khi giá vàng liên tục tăng cao, chị không dám mua vì lo ngại rủi ro. Nay giá vàng đã hạ nhiệt, chị lại băn khoăn liệu đây có phải thời điểm thích hợp để mua vào hay giá sẽ tiếp tục đi xuống.
“Giá vàng đã giảm khá nhiều so với năm ngoái, tôi đang tính mua một ít để dành. Nhưng mua lúc này lại sợ giá tiếp tục giảm, còn chờ thêm thì lo giá tăng trở lại. Không biết có nên mua ngay hay đợi thêm một thời gian”, chị Hạnh chia sẻ.
Theo bảng giá của SJC, ngày 6/11/2026, vàng miếng SJC được niêm yết ở mức 138 triệu đồng/lượng chiều mua vào và 141 triệu đồng/lượng chiều bán ra. So với mức bán ra 148,4 triệu đồng/lượng cùng ngày năm 2025, giá vàng miếng đã giảm khoảng 5%.
Đối với vàng nhẫn trơn 9999, giá bán giữa các thương hiệu có sự khác biệt. Chẳng hạn, vàng nhẫn PNJ 9999 ngày 6/11/2026 được niêm yết ở mức 140,3 triệu đồng/lượng chiều bán ra, trong khi cùng kỳ năm ngoái dao động từ 145,8-148,8 triệu đồng/lượng.
Có nên mua vàng thời điểm này?
Ông Nguyễn Mạnh Cường, chuyên viên tư vấn tài chính, cho rằng giá vàng giảm so với cùng kỳ năm trước có thể tạo cơ hội cho những người muốn mua tích trữ dài hạn. Tuy nhiên, nhà đầu tư không nên vội vàng xuống tiền chỉ vì cho rằng giá vàng đã giảm sâu và sắp tăng trở lại.
Với trường hợp của chị Bích Hạnh, người đang có khoản tiền tiết kiệm 100 triệu đồng, điều quan trọng trước tiên là xác định mục đích sử dụng khoản tiền này. Nếu đây là tiền nhàn rỗi, chưa có nhu cầu sử dụng trong ít nhất 1-3 năm tới và đã có khoản dự phòng cho những tình huống phát sinh, chị có thể cân nhắc dành một phần để tích lũy vàng.
Ngược lại, nếu 100 triệu đồng là khoản tiết kiệm chủ yếu của gia đình, còn phục vụ chi tiêu thiết yếu hoặc các kế hoạch ngắn hạn, việc dồn toàn bộ số tiền vào vàng sẽ tiềm ẩn nhiều rủi ro.
Người mua nên cân nhắc phương pháp tích lũy từng phần thay vì sử dụng toàn bộ số tiền để mua tại một thời điểm. Với khoản tiền 100 triệu đồng, chị Hạnh có thể xem xét dành khoảng 20-30 triệu đồng để mua vàng, phần còn lại gửi tiết kiệm hoặc phân bổ vào các kênh đầu tư phù hợp. Việc chia nhỏ khoản tiền mua vàng theo từng thời điểm giúp hạn chế rủi ro khi giá tiếp tục giảm.
Một yếu tố khác cần đặc biệt lưu ý là chênh lệch giữa giá mua vào và bán ra. Ngày 6/11/2026, giá vàng miếng SJC được niêm yết ở mức 138 triệu đồng/lượng chiều mua vào và 141 triệu đồng/lượng chiều bán ra, chênh lệch 3 triệu đồng/lượng.
Điều đó đồng nghĩa với việc người mua có thể chịu khoản lỗ khoảng 2% ngay sau giao dịch nếu bán lại khi giá thị trường chưa thay đổi. Vì vậy, những người có ý định mua vàng để lướt sóng trong vài tuần hoặc vài tháng cần hết sức thận trọng.
Đối với người mua vàng tích trữ, vàng nhẫn trơn 9999 là một lựa chọn có thể cân nhắc nhờ có nhiều quy cách trọng lượng, phù hợp với nhu cầu tích lũy định kỳ. Tuy nhiên, người mua cần lựa chọn thương hiệu uy tín, kiểm tra hóa đơn, chất lượng sản phẩm và tìm hiểu chính sách thu mua lại trước khi giao dịch.
Ngoài ra, ông Cường lưu ý không nên vay tiền để mua vàng hoặc sử dụng toàn bộ khoản tiết kiệm dự phòng để tìm cách bắt đáy. Dù được nhiều người lựa chọn như một kênh tích trữ tài sản, vàng vẫn có thể trải qua những giai đoạn giảm giá kéo dài và không tạo ra nguồn thu nhập định kỳ.
Với những người đang phân vân như chị Hạnh, lời khuyên là không cần cố gắng xác định chính xác đâu là đáy của giá vàng. Thay vào đó, nên mua từng phần bằng nguồn tiền thực sự nhàn rỗi, duy trì khoản dự phòng cần thiết và xác định thời gian nắm giữ dài hạn.

articles.title: Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning - Engadget
articles.text:
Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
With a bit of cleaning and system management, you can keep your laptop fan from jump-scaring you.
You're sitting down with your laptop in front of you, getting a bit of light work done, when suddenly you hear what sounds like a jet engine going off. Your computer's fans start roaring and whirring, but after a short moment, everything is quiet again. If you've ever had your laptop fan sound off without warning like this, there are a few possible causes.
Over the years, laptops have become much better at managing performance and cooling, but even the best laptops of today need strong fans to keep their high-powered components cool in such a compact space. While some fan noise is perfectly normal, persistent or unusually loud bursts can indicate that your laptop is working harder than it needs to. Sudden spikes in fan noise are often caused by intensive background activity or dust restricting airflow. Both are relatively easy to investigate, and there are a few simple ways to check what's making your laptop work harder and address the problem.
How to check and clean your laptop fan
The first thing to check if your laptop fan starts acting up is whether it's getting enough airflow. Make sure you're using it on a hard, flat surface like a table or desk rather than a bed, sofa, or other soft surface that could block its vents. If the fan continues to run loudly, dust buildup around the fans or air vents could be the issue.
Luckily, you can typically clean your fans and air vents without taking the machine apart. First, turn off your laptop, unplug any attached devices, and wait for it to cool. Then locate the air vents, which may be on the underside or sides of the device, depending on the model. Use short bursts of compressed air to dislodge dust and debris, following the instructions on the can. You can then wipe away any loose debris with a clean microfiber cloth.
If this approach doesn't do the trick, you may need to dismantle your laptop for greater access to the fans. Along with compressed air, you can also use an ESD-safe brush to remove dust from the components. This process may be a little advanced for some users, and the exact method depends on the type of laptop you're working with. If you're not comfortable taking apart your laptop yourself, it's worth getting in touch with a technician. Also, before dismantling the machine, check your warranty terms and manufacturer's guidance on user repairs, as opening the laptop or carrying out repairs yourself may affect your coverage.
How to check for intensive background activity
If your laptop's fans continue to get extra loud at random intervals, it's possible the CPU is getting a covert workout. On Windows, tap Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager and select Processes to see what's running. Click the CPU column to sort processes by how much processing power they're using, putting the biggest resource hogs at the top. Then, head to Startup apps and disable any programs you don't want launching automatically when you start your laptop. If you're a Mac user, open Activity Monitor (hit Command+Spacebar to open Spotlight Search if you're struggling to find it) and head to CPU to identify the processes using the most resources. Click the % CPU column to sort them, then select a process and click the Stop button, then choose Quit.
Before you get trigger-happy, look out for background processes you can live without instead of quitting them willy-nilly (as doing so can lead to some big crashes). On Windows, if you're not using programs like Calculator, Gaming Services, News and Interests, Phone Link, CTF Loader or Groove Music, you can generally end their processes. On Mac, you can quit lingering processes associated with apps you've already closed, Rosetta applications you're no longer using and disk image processes that are preventing a disk from ejecting. You can also disable Spotlight indexing if you don't need your Mac to maintain a fully indexed library.

articles.title: Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
articles.text:
Soul Glo has a new record called NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it’s not enough to truly tide me over, so I’ve been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 — Diaspora Problems.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
“Gold Chain Punk (whogonbeatmyass?)” is an opening salvo for the ages. Bong rip, into a catchy-as-hell hardcore riff, with frontman Pierce Jordan ranting. Then comes the half-time stomp as Jordan gets fully unhinged, screaming “Who gon beat my ass? Who the fuck gon beat my ass?” From here on out, as the music shifts through a few different sections, the energy never comes down. Jordan shreds his vocal cords, begging, “Can I live?” Before finally spelling it out for anyone still confused:
Say more, say less, it’s all the same
When it’s time to die we can meet outside
To see who gon feel my pain
The record barely lets up from here on out. “Coming Correct” opens with a cough and a steady 808, giving you literally three seconds to catch your breath before Jordan jumps on the mic shouting, “I try to listen the way, I wanna be listened to.” The song starts stacking elements quickly, reaching full firestorm by 25 seconds in, and then does let up for the rest of its three-minute runtime.
The front chunk of the record is just perfect unrelenting hardcore song after perfect unrelenting hardcore song. Jordan’s crazed charisma is undeniable as he ricochets between leftist rhetoric, goofy bits about smoking weed, and vulnerable explorations of his struggles with depression. You’d be forgiven for struggling to keep up with his rapid-fire delivery, which owes almost as much to modern rappers as it does to classic hardcore acts like Minor Threat or Bad Brains.
Track six, “Driponomics,” fully embraces those more modern influences with trap snares, wall-rattling 808 kicks, and a guest verse from Mother Maryrose. The sampled guitar calls to mind the sax squeals favored by the Bomb Squad… just heavier.
The album eventually culminates in “Spiritual Level Of Gang Shit,” which features guest verses from McKinley Dixon and Lojii over gently echoed guitar melodies and dub-inspired groove. Then, around the 2:20 mark, things take a turn as the guitars turn punishing and the drums shift to a standard hardcore beat. But the song hasn’t reached its final form yet. That comes almost a minute later when the horn section kicks in.
Next to other modern hardcore standard bearers like Turnstile, Soul Glo might almost seem like traditionalists heavily influenced by the DC scene. But Diaspora Problems shows their ambition and willingness to take risks. Soul Glo plays with genre, is confrontational in its politics, and is generally just uncompromising.
Oh, and they put on a hell of a live show (I’ve seen them at least four times now). Don’t miss their incredible Tiny Desk Concert either, which I’m pretty sure is the first mosh pit to even open up in the NPR offices.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Qobuz, Deezer, YouTube Music, Apple Music, and Spotify.

articles.title: Decathlon mở cửa hàng thứ 10 tại Dĩ An
articles.text:
Decathlon mở cửa hàng thứ 10 tại GO! Dĩ An, đúng dịp tròn 7 năm ở Việt Nam.
Ngày 7/11, hai con lân xanh và một hàng nhân viên áo xanh đứng trước dải băng khai trương ở tầng trệt Trung tâm thương mại GO! Dĩ An. Đây là cửa hàng thứ 10 của Decathlon tại Việt Nam, và cũng là lần đầu thương hiệu thể thao đến từ Pháp này có mặt tại khu vực Bình Dương cũ.
Cột mốc rơi đúng năm thứ 7 Decathlon làm bán lẻ ở Việt Nam. Năm 2026 cũng là năm thương hiệu này tròn 50 tuổi trên toàn cầu.
Từ chuỗi cung ứng tới 10 cửa hàng
Decathlon có mặt ở Việt Nam từ năm 1995, nhưng suốt gần 25 năm đầu hãng chỉ hiện diện qua chuỗi cung ứng sản xuất. Phải tới năm 2019, cửa hàng bán lẻ đầu tiên mới mở cửa đón khách.
Kim chỉ nam của hãng trên chặng đường ấy là khẩu hiệu “Thể thao cho tất cả, tất cả vì thể thao”. Theo Decathlon, đồ tập đạt chuẩn quốc tế không nhất thiết phải đi cùng một mức giá đắt đỏ.
Vì sao điểm thứ 10 là Dĩ An
Decathlon chọn Dĩ An vì đây là cửa ngõ nối khu vực Bình Dương cũ với trung tâm TP.HCM, nơi tập trung đông cư dân trẻ, người lao động và các gia đình. Theo Tuổi Trẻ, phường Dĩ An hiện là phường đông dân nhất TP.HCM với hơn 256.000 người.
Ông Gregory Fontugne, Giám đốc Khối Cửa hàng Decathlon Việt Nam, cho rằng việc có mặt tại Dĩ An “không đơn thuần là mở thêm một điểm bán”. Theo ông, đây là một bước trong nỗ lực “xóa bỏ rào cản về chi phí”, để sản phẩm thể thao chuẩn Pháp hợp hơn với ngân sách của mọi gia đình Việt.
472m² cho hơn 60 môn thể thao
Cửa hàng Decathlon Dĩ An rộng 472m² và bày đồ cho hơn 60 môn thể thao. Khách có thể tìm từ đồ chạy bộ, bóng đá, cầu lông, bơi lội và thể hình cho buổi tập thường ngày, tới trang bị trekking, leo núi và cắm trại cho những chuyến đi xa.
Nhóm sản phẩm được hãng đưa lên đầu gồm kính bơi có tròng theo độ cận và chống đọng sương, đồ bơi chống nắng, áo khoác gió Helium siêu nhẹ cùng đồ trekking. Theo Decathlon, nhiều món tại cửa hàng có giá từ vài chục tới vài trăm nghìn đồng.
Ông Bảo Adams, Giám đốc Cửa hàng Decathlon Dĩ An, cho biết mục tiêu mang thể thao và sức khỏe tới mọi người đã được hãng theo đuổi tại hơn 82 quốc gia và vùng lãnh thổ. Ở Dĩ An, đội ngũ của ông muốn cùng người dân địa phương “biến việc rèn luyện thể chất thành niềm vui mỗi ngày”.
Quà khai trương theo từng hóa đơn
Trong hai ngày 7/11 và 8/11, 50 khách đến sớm nhất mỗi ngày được tặng một ba lô Decathlon mà không cần mua hàng. Mỗi hóa đơn trong hai ngày này còn kèm một lượt chơi minigame để nhận voucher.
Từ 7/11 tới hết 11/11, hóa đơn từ 299.000 đồng được tặng túi mua sắm Decathlon. Hóa đơn từ 499.000 đồng nhận ba lô thể thao 17L, món quà trị giá 245.000 đồng. Ở mức hóa đơn tối thiểu, giá trị món quà này tương đương gần một nửa số tiền khách bỏ ra.
Chuỗi ưu đãi khai trương kéo dài tới hết ngày 11/11, còn quà tặng có thể hết sớm hơn vì số lượng có hạn. Với một thương hiệu vừa tròn nửa thế kỷ, 10 cửa hàng sau 7 năm là nhịp mở rộng từ tốn, nhưng mỗi điểm mới lại đưa đồ tập chuẩn quốc tế tới gần một cộng đồng trước đó chưa có cửa hàng Decathlon nào ở gần. Cửa hàng ở Dĩ An đặt kệ đồ tập ngay cạnh nơi các gia đình đi siêu thị cuối tuần, và quãng đường ngắn ấy mới là thước đo thật của lời hứa thể thao cho tất cả.
* Thông tin cửa hàng, ưu đãi và phát biểu theo thông cáo báo chí của Decathlon Việt Nam ngày 7/11/2026. Ảnh: Decathlon Việt Nam. Quà tặng có số lượng có hạn và chương trình có thể kết thúc sớm khi hết quà.
* Từ ngày 1/7/2025, Dĩ An thuộc TP.HCM sau đợt sắp xếp đơn vị hành chính, nên bài dùng cách gọi khu vực Bình Dương cũ. Dân số phường Dĩ An theo Tuổi Trẻ. Trục thời gian ở khối 01 vẽ đúng tỉ lệ. Mô hình ở khối 02 chia khu theo nhóm môn để minh họa, không phải mặt bằng thật của cửa hàng. Tỉ lệ quà trên hóa đơn ở khối 03 do Finelines tính từ mức hóa đơn tối thiểu.

articles.title: Don't throw away your old flip phone – do this instead - Engadget
articles.text:
Don't throw away your old flip phone – do this instead
There's plenty you can do with an old flip phone instead of retiring it.
So, you are doing a bit of seasonal cleaning, and you came across the dreaded electronics drawer. One minute you are blissfully tidying up your office, the next you are confronted with a mountainous trove of old gadgets. But don't worry, holding onto an old flip phone is not a surefire sign that you belong on the next episode of "Hoarders."
Despite their lack of advanced features, old cellphones can still serve utilitarian purposes in their old age. From serving as an emergency backup to saving you from crafty pickpockets on vacation, you probably have good reasons to keep your old phones around.
But saving your phone is more than a useful lifehack: It's an ecological imperative. The mass of e-waste mounting in global landfills is an underdiscussed crisis. According to the United Nations' e-Waste Monitor, an estimated 62 million tons of electronics were thrown into the trash heap in 2022, representing an 82% increase from the decade prior. The UN projects yearly e-waste to increase by another 32% by 2030. Containing non-biodegradable materials and toxic chemicals, this mass of e-waste poses an acute danger to our air, water, and soil. Waste from the US alone was found to be causing a "hidden tsunami" of junk in Southeast Asia.
The vast majority of this waste goes unrecycled. According to the UN, less than a quarter of global electronic waste is correctly processed. Luckily, it is easy to recycle your old phone or donate it to charitable organizations in desperate need of cell phones. So if you need to declutter your office, there are an abundance of options that don't involve consigning your device to the global scrap heap.
Repurposing your flip phone
Rather than firing your old flip phone, simply reassign it to a new role. One option is to make your old phone an emergency backup. Notably, this doesn't require you to pay for an active SIM card, either, as all cellular phones in the US can call 911, no matter their carrier status. Keeping an extra phone in your household's emergency response kit will help ensure that you are always able to contact emergency services. Just make sure that it is charged, turned off, and easily accessible in the case of an emergency.
It is important to acknowledge that there are some caveats when using a SIM-less phone in an emergency. When a 911 call is made from an uninitialized phone, dispatchers at the call center are unable to receive critical location information, such as the address from which you called. Moreover, the 911 center won't be able to return your call if you are disconnected. Being aware of these limitations will help you communicate more effectively with first responders.
You can also use a flip phone as a backup dumbphone, which is incredibly useful for instances in which you might damage or lose your smartphone. For instance, dumbphones can be a lifesaver during outdoor activities where your electronics might get wet, such as water sports, fishing trips, or beach days. Longer battery life also makes them a lifesaver during overnight camping trips. Second phones are also helpful when traveling to places where you may have your phone stolen or simply lose it. As a global traveler, having a phone you don't mind losing can be a major luxury when vacationing in crowded cities or events. Unlike your emergency phone, however, you will need a SIM card to swap into your dumb phone as needed.
Donating your phone
If you want to reduce your excess gadgets, there are countless organizations that repurpose used cellphones for a worthy cause. Secure The Call is exemplary of how repurposed gadgets can be used to save lives, providing free 911 emergency phones and tablets to victims of domestic violence, senior citizens, and other high-risk communities. To date, the nonprofit has delivered over 50,000 cellphones to people in need. Other national organizations include More Than A Phone, the 911CellPhoneBank, and Verizon's HopeLine, which operates out of your local Verizon store.
Another notable donation program is Cell Phones For Soldiers, which provides cost-free communication tools and emergency assistance to veterans and active-duty military personnel. Through its Minutes That Matter program, Cell Phones For Soldiers has delivered 8 million prepaid calling cards to active-duty service members overseas, helping them connect with family and friends during difficult deployments. In 2024, the nonprofit began delivering phones to homeless and low-income veterans. In just two years, the nonprofit has delivered 14,500 phones to veterans in need, helping them connect to essential services, loved ones, and potential job opportunities.
Several national organizations help you recycle your used phone and unwanted gadgets, such as The Salvation Army and Goodwill. Large tech chains, like Best Buy and Staples, also offer recycling programs. One helpful resource is the Consumer Technology Association's GreenerGadgets. An online resource aimed at educating consumers about environmental issues, GreenerGadgets has an online search tool to help you find the nearest electronics recycling location. The tool also connects you with mail-back and repair programs. Simply add your zip code and electronic device type to search for a donation center near you. Earth911 is a similar organization that connects you to donation centers with a simple search function.

articles.text:

Thời gian cập nhật: 06:00-8/11/2026
Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 8/11
Đầu tuần, giá vàng giá vàng thế giới giao dịch quanh 3.875 USD/ounce. Kim loại quý được hỗ trợ bởi giá dầu giảm, góp phần hạ bớt lo ngại lạm phát, cùng lực mua bắt đáy.
Đà phục hồi mạnh hơn sau khi đảng Dân chủ giành quyền kiểm soát cả Thượng viện và Hạ viện Mỹ. Kết quả này làm gia tăng kỳ vọng về khả năng bế tắc lập pháp và những thay đổi trong triển vọng ngân sách. Đồng USD và lợi suất trái phiếu suy yếu trong một số phiên, tạo thêm động lực cho giá vàng vượt mốc 4.000 USD/ounce.
Đến thứ Năm, vàng giao ngay lập đỉnh tuần tại 4.147 USD/ounce. Tuy nhiên, làn sóng bán tháo cổ phiếu công nghệ khiến nhà đầu tư tiếp tục thanh lý tài sản trên nhiều thị trường.
Áp lực bán gia tăng trong phiên 6/11, sau khi báo cáo việc làm tháng 10 của Mỹ được công bố.
Theo Cục Thống kê Lao động Mỹ, nền kinh tế tạo thêm 165.000 việc làm phi nông nghiệp trong tháng, cao hơn đáng kể so với dự báo khoảng 65.000 việc làm. Số liệu này củng cố kỳ vọng Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) có thể tăng lãi suất trong tháng 12, đẩy đồng USD và lợi suất trái phiếu ngắn hạn đi lên.
Nếu chỉ số lạm phát công bố tuần tới tiếp tục cao, lợi suất trái phiếu và đồng USD có thể tăng, gây sức ép khiến vàng lùi xuống dưới 4.000 USD/ounce.
Giá vàng có lúc lùi về gần 4.030 USD/ounce, trước khi phục hồi nhẹ lên sát 4.070 USD/ounce vào cuối tuần.
Chốt tuần, giá vàng giao ngay ở mức 4.072 USD/ounce. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 12/2026 giao dịch quanh mức 4.079 USD/ounce.
Tại thị trường trong nước, vàng miếng SJC ngày 7/11 được niêm yết ở mức 138 triệu đồng/lượng mua vào và 141 triệu đồng/lượng bán ra. So với cuối tuần trước, giá bán ra tăng khoảng 2 triệu đồng/lượng.
Các chuyên gia dự báo giá vàng có thể tiếp tục biến động mạnh trong tuần tới. Một số phân tích kỹ thuật xem vùng 4.000 USD/ounce là ngưỡng hỗ trợ đáng chú ý, trong khi khu vực 4.170 USD/ounce là vùng kháng cự cần vượt qua để củng cố đà tăng.
Số liệu lạm phát Mỹ sẽ tác động lớn đến kỳ vọng lãi suất Fed và xu hướng giá vàng. Về dài hạn, triển vọng vàng vẫn được hỗ trợ bởi nhu cầu mua của ngân hàng trung ương và bất ổn địa chính trị.

articles.title: Epic Games Launcher is coming to SteamOS
articles.text:
In October, Epic Games said that it was “investigating” making Fortnite compatible with Valve’s Linux-based SteamOS. At the time, Epic Games Launcher was in preview, but SteamOS was not specifically listed as a supported distro. Now, Communications Director Jake Jones has confirmed SteamOS compatibility, along with a handful of other distros, to GamingOnLinux. In response to a question about the AppImage being replaced with Debian / Ubuntu .deb downloads, Jones said:
Epic Games Launcher is coming to SteamOS
Epic Games confirmed that its Linux launcher will officially support SteamOS and Steam Decks.
“The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We’re testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we’ll restore AppImage this month.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean Fortnite will come to SteamOS. Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2 support still remains an open question. When it announced its work to bring Fortnite to Linux, the company said that the Steam Deck “does not support the required features for our EAC v2 solution, but we are actively talking with Valve and hope to support it in the future.”

articles.title: Tencent AI chief warns of AI biology risks, SCMP reports
articles.text:
Tencent’s chief AI scientist has warned that AI models will soon be able to cause harm in biology, as they already can in cybersecurity. Yao Shunyu spoke at a science event in Hong Kong on Saturday, the South China Morning Post reported.
“The cyber abilities of [AI] models and soon [the] bio ability of models will reach a threshold where it’s actually possible to do harm,” Yao said, according to the SCMP.
He said Chinese companies that release open models, which anyone can download and change, need to take safety very seriously. He also warned that biology risks may be harder to manage than cyber risks.
Yao, 29, joined Tencent last year after a year at OpenAI. He spoke days after Tencent launched Hy4, its new flagship model, on 4 November.
In its launch announcement, Tencent said it left material on exploiting software flaws out of Hy4’s training data. The model was instead trained on defensive security data, the company said.
Tencent also said that Hy4 has strong basic knowledge of biology, but is weaker than leading models at designing experiments. It said it based this on internal expert reviews. TNW has not tested the model.
The company plans to release Hy4’s weights and a report on its safety testing in the coming days, Reuters reported. Hy4 ranks as the second-best Chinese model, according to benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis, the SCMP said.
Yao said US firms such as Anthropic make a strong case for keeping top models closed. However, he argued that a mix of open and closed models may work best, because open models can also help defenders.

articles.title: The danger of charging your phone under your pillow isn't radiation - Engadget
articles.text:
The danger of charging your phone under your pillow isn't radiation
You won’t get cancer, but you might catch fire if you keep doing this.
You've probably heard this warning before: Never sleep with your phone under the pillow; your brain will get all the radiation, and you'll develop cancer. Well, a World Health Organization (WHO)-commissioned study from two years ago says that's quite unlikely, so you don't have to worry about cancer if you end up tucking the phone under your head for the night. You should, however, be concerned about your phone overheating and the risks of it causing a fire.
It's quite understandable that, after finally finishing scrolling social media or whatever it is you do before bed, you'd want to tuck that phone away wherever it's closest to you. That's either right next to your head or under your pillow, if you want to ensure you won't slap it into the next dimension in your sleep. The problem is that, if your phone is also charging, its temperature will rise. With it tucked under your pillow, the growing heat can't dissipate into the open air like it normally would. Over time, this can damage your device, shorten the battery's lifespan and, in some rare but documented cases, lead to burns or fires. Understanding why this happens and what to do instead can help protect both your phone and your home without giving up the convenience of keeping your device nearby.
Overheating, not radiation, is the real risk
Charging your phone is very much a thermal process. Lithium-ion batteries, which nearly all smartphones use nowadays, release heat as they draw power. That heat needs to dissipate safely, and it needs a hard, open surface to do this without issue. When you keep your phone in bed with you, under a pillow, a blanket, or anywhere airflow is restricted, that doesn't happen.
If you do it a handful of times, this won't be an issue, but if it happens repeatedly, there can be consequences you won't like. Your device's battery will degrade faster, as prolonged heat exposure accelerates the breakdown of battery cells. Diminishing battery performance on smartphones is already a touchy subject for most users, so speed-running that process doesn't sound like a good idea.
That excess heat won't just damage your phone's battery, but it can also warp components or trigger safety shutdowns. Repeated overheating increases the odds of permanent hardware problems. In rare cases, trapped heat combined with a damaged battery can lead to what's called thermal runaway, where your phone starts generating heat faster than it can get rid of it. At this point, the phone is at high risk of catching fire. If you're also using an uncertified charger that lacks proper heat regulation and surge protection, overheating is even more likely to happen. The solution to this problem is pretty straightforward, and it's to simply place your phone on a hard, flat and well-ventilated surface when you're charging it.
What about radiation?
We've all heard warnings about phones and radiation risk. Some voices say not to sleep with your phone under the pillow; others say it shouldn't even be on the nightstand near your head, while some even insist that the phone shouldn't be in the room with you at all.
The reality is that cell phones emit non-ionizing radiofrequency radiation, which is a low-energy form of radiation that doesn't carry enough strength to damage DNA the way X-rays or gamma rays can. Over the years, research has been done extensively on this topic. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Environment International Journal found "moderate-certainty evidence that it likely does not increase the risk of glioma, meningioma, acoustic neuroma, pituitary tumors, and salivary gland tumours in adults, or of paediatric brain tumors." Basically, chances are slim you'll get any type of head tumor from your phone.
This doesn't mean that reducing exposure isn't worth practicing. Fire and overheating, however, are the more likely risks that deserve your attention first.
Develop safer charging habits
If you want to mitigate the risk of your phone's battery swelling overnight, you need to be more careful with your phone and how you're charging it. First of all, you should have a bedside table or desk nearby where you can charge your phone on a hard, open surface. Even the floor beside your bed is a better idea if you have hard floors.
You could also get a wireless charging pad to place on your nightstand, so your device always has a designated nap spot. Make sure you're only using certified chargers while you're at it. You might also want to switch to a classic alarm clock for morning wake-ups so you're no longer tempted to bring your phone as close to your ear as possible.
These changes take very little effort on your part but will reduce the odds of battery damage, device failure, or, even worse, fire. You'll still get to use your phone before bed and charge it overnight, but you'll do it all safely.

articles.title: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy
articles.text:
Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:
Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy
Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec the company is opening an investigation.
The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing.
Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have restricted their sale to China. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.
Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

articles.title: Italy blames pro-Russian hackers for Tajani data leak
articles.text:
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has blamed pro-Russian hackers for posting the foreign minister’s personal data on the dark web. She said the sale of officials’ data was a grave concern, in a statement carried by ANSA on Saturday.
The minister, Antonio Tajani, said on X that the hackers had been spreading his data for days. He said they also wanted more facts about him and his family, and would pay for them.
He said Italy’s support for Ukraine was the reason he had been targeted.
“I will not be intimidated in any way,” Tajani wrote, in TNW’s translation.
Neither of them named a group. But the Italian paper Il Fatto Quotidiano said the data was posted by NoName057(16), a pro-Russian hacking group, according to LaPresse. TNW has not confirmed this.
NoName057(16) is best known for flooding websites with traffic to knock them offline. In May, Dutch police seized 800 servers linked to the group.
Other officials were also targeted, LaPresse reported. They include Rome’s chief prosecutor, Francesco Lo Voi, and Ivano Gabrielli, who heads Italy’s cyber police. Rome prosecutors are investigating, it added, citing Il Fatto Quotidiano.
Tajani wants hybrid attacks at the top of the agenda at a G7 meeting in Paris on Monday, Bloomberg reported, citing ANSA. The Kremlin did not respond to Bloomberg.

articles.title: Suno AI music generator sued again for copyright infringement - Engadget
articles.text:
Suno AI music generator sued again for copyright infringement
Groups that own the music rights to Elvis Presley and Eminem’s tracks filed the latest lawsuits.
New lawsuits are claiming that Suno has once again committed copyright infringement by using Elvis Presley and Eminem's likeness to create AI-generated songs. As first reported by Variety, a group that owns the rights to Presley's music and Eight Mile Style, a music publishing company that owns hundreds of Eminem recordings, filed separate lawsuits against Suno. Both lawsuits offered examples of songs created through the AI music generator that allegedly sound like Presley or mimic Eminem's lyrics.
A group of attorneys representing the plaintiffs in each case said that Suno's actions "make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect." Suno countered with a statement to Variety that said it doesn't allow "any unauthorized use of an artist's work," specifying that it prohibits using "specific artists' names and songs," while also working with third-party companies to screen for "potential misuse."
The group behind Presley's music rights has set it sights on combating AI copyright infringement. It recently filed a lawsuit against Anthropic, claiming $41 million in damages for allegedly training its AI models on the musician's works without permission.
As for Suno, these lawsuits are the latest addition to its existing list of copyright infringement accusations. Earlier this year, Sony Music Entertainment and Universal Music Group jointly filed another lawsuit claiming that Suno is still infringing on its copyrighted material for its latest v6 models. However, not all record labels and publishing companies are continuing their legal actions. Last year, Warner Music Group decided to drop its lawsuit against Suno, instead agreeing to a licensing deal.

articles.title: I Used NYT Cooking’s New AI-Powered Recipe Modifier, and It’s Actually Pretty Good
articles.text:
In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.
I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.
Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.
After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.
The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.
My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.
Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.
Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.
Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.
If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.
"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.
For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."
She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.
When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."
So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.
As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.
I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.
Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.
It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.
This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.
From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.
I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.
A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.
Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.
Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.
It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?
Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.
It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.
That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

articles.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
articles.text:
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.
Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.
But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:
Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

articles.title: CoreWeave writes to Texas governor-elect on data centres
articles.text:
I cloud company CoreWeave has written to Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, offering to work with her team on data centre rules. The letter from chief executive Michael Intrator was sent on Saturday, Bloomberg reported.
Intrator offered to work with her transition team on finishing projects that already have permits. He also offered help setting clear, lasting standards for new ones, Bloomberg reported.
Hinojosa, a Democrat, won Tuesday’s election after promising to pause new data centres until the state has rules for them. She has said they should pay their own way and put Texans’ water and power first, ABC13 reported.
CoreWeave appears to expect that projects already approved can go ahead. Carl Holshouser, its head of government affairs, said in a LinkedIn post that Hinojosa had made clear permitted projects can be completed.
TNW could not find Hinojosa saying this herself. Her team has not said how a pause would work.
Holshouser, who helped write the letter, said families should not pay for new power lines and plants. He added that new sites should protect local water and power.
Texas has already got tougher. In August, outgoing Governor Greg Abbott ordered regulators to pause new grid links and start auditing data centres.

articles.title: Why 2TB of phone storage makes more sense than you think - Engadget
articles.text:
Why 2TB of phone storage makes more sense than you think
Here's who should spend the extra money on a 2TB phone and who should skip it.
For most people, a 2TB smartphone is a bit of overkill since they won't actually need that much storage space. Unless you shoot professional-grade videos, edit long-form content or download a ton of games, a more modest storage option is better, especially given how expensive it is to buy the 2TB models.
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro with 256GB of storage starts at $1,199, but the 2TB model costs twice as much. The flashy new iPhone Duo is already $1,999 for its 256GB model, but it's a steep $3,199 for the 2TB version. That's a $1,200 premium that most people won't need to pay.
With photos automatically backing up to the cloud, streaming apps replacing downloaded media and social apps and messaging tools taking up less space than a decade ago, 2TB doesn't make sense for the average consumer. For most folks, a 128GB or 256GB phone covers daily use for pics, apps, music and the occasional episode downloaded for in-flight entertainment.
So why does the 2TB exist at all? Content creators who take full advantage of the iPhone camera, gamers storing multiple games that together take up over 100GB of space and people who don't want to hand their personal pictures and videos to iCloud are just some users who can justify paying extra. These buyers don't have to constantly delete files, uninstall apps or juggle external drives.
Who actually needs 2TB of phone storage?
We're going to mainly talk about iPhone users here since you can't get Android smartphones with 2TB of built-in storage. Some Samsung and Sony phones do let you expand storage with a microSD card up to 2TB, but most apps can't be moved to the microSD, so that card only makes sense if you change the default folder.
So what are the use cases that would justify spending an extra $1,200? Shooting ProRes RAW video tops the list here. Apple says a minute of full-sensor ProRes RAW at 30 fps can use more than 10GB, and ProRes RAW HQ can use more than 15GB, so a 10-minute take can approach or pass 100GB. Anything less than 1TB is impractical for serious video work, especially since you'll probably need to shoot multiple takes.
Professional photographers face similar problems. Shooting in RAW format rather than compressed JPEG produces files that are up to 10 times larger; maintaining a working library of originals also adds up fast. Video editors working on vlogs, documentaries or short films also need lots of storage. You'll also need some elbow room to edit footage directly on a phone without constant file management.
If you're into downloading movies and shows for travel, you can fill a phone quickly, especially without reliable Wi-Fi. A single film can run 3GB to 4GB, so a handful of movies plus a few seasons of a show adds up fast. If you're a gamer, some titles can range from 20GB to 40GB and use quite a bit of your storage. Even a modest library of titles can consume a big chunk of a 256GB device.
How much storage do you actually need?
When deciding how much storage to buy, think about how you'll use your phone. Cloud storage can be a solution, but it does have limitations. ProRes video, for instance, can't record directly to iCloud or similar services in real time; videos must first be captured locally, then uploaded or transferred. When you're shooting in remote locations or areas with poor connectivity, you won't be able to send footage to the cloud to make room for new videos.
General consumers who take a few pics every day, install some apps, stream movies on occasion and play a couple of games should be able to get away with 128 or 256GB of space. Power users and gamers who want the room to install all the apps and games they want will be better off with 512GB. Pro creators, however, should shoot for 1TB or 2TB models so they don't have to rely on external storage.

articles.title: Wandrd’s Magnetic Camera Straps Are My New Favorite Accessory
articles.text:
More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting systems that make it hard to quickly remove the strap from the camera when you need to, like when you're attaching your camera to a tripod or gimbal and you’d rather not have a dangling strap whacking you in the face.
Peak Design solved this with its Anchor Links system, small circular nubs you leave attached to camera eyelets that make detaching or even swapping straps easy. The quick-connect mechanism is now the de facto industry standard and has inspired countless copycats.
Now, Wandrd has outdone that design using magnets.
“We're photographers ourselves, so we're constantly ideating, tinkering, thinking of ways that things can be better,” Ryan Cope, Wandrd cofounder, tells WIRED. “A camera strap like this has been at the back of our minds for a while.”
Wandrd—known for its camera bags—launched its Magnetic Camera Strap system on Thursday. It features a circular anchor similar to Peak Design, called “Torus Links.” The anchors attach to your camera’s eyelets and are rated to carry up to 198 pounds—so unless you're bench-pressing your camera, they'll do the job. If the cord does start to wear down over time, you'll first see yellow under the black fabric—a sign you should replace the Torus Link. If it's red, you should stop using the link immediately—a warning system borrowed from Peak Design. (Wandrd offers a two-year warranty.)
Unlike Peak Design's anchors, the Wandrd anchors look like donuts, with a hole in the middle. When you attach the strap, the embedded magnets guide the Torus Link into the strap's CoreLock mechanism, which pinches into the hole to secure the camera body. The magnets make connecting a strap easier, and they keep the strap fastened to the anchor, but you can’t just pull the strap off like you’re pulling a MagSafe accessory on your phone. You’ll need to use the strap’s dual-pinch mechanism to remove it from the Torus Link, a design that’s more secure.
It’s a much faster way to connect and disconnect a strap, and that speed pays off in the field. This week, I had to photograph a product during a press briefing. Usually, I use Peak Design's Leash and, instead of taking off the strap, I bunch it up in my hand when it's not around my neck. It's not that it's hard to remove—it's just an extra step I have to think about. But Wandrd's magnetic system felt faster to unlock mid-shoot when I wanted to lower the camera for an awkward, low-angle shot, and reattaching the strap was practically instantaneous. I did the whole swap one-handed, with the magnets doing most of the work.
“I love magnets, man,” Cope says. “I love the simplicity they create—guiding things into place. You don't always have a place to put your camera down; I like that magnets help guide them and are a lot more secure, and they're also just fun.”
I have two Torus Links on my camera body, one on the right eyelet and another on the tripod baseplate. But my favorite configuration turns the strap into a single-point sling. The strap has a built-in “Torus Loop” on the buckle—clip one end directly into it to create a closed loop worn across your torso, leaving just a single magnetic connector to snap onto your camera. When you unclip the camera to shoot freely, the strap stays neatly in place across your body instead of sliding off your shoulder.
The nylon felt comfortable across my chest and near my neck—there's no padding, but that's intentional. Cope says Wandrd spent two years developing this custom “liquid nylon” tubular webbing that is softer along the edges, so it won't feel like the strap is cutting into your neck after a long day of wear. The lack of metal throughout the strap system also prevents the strap from scratching up your camera gear.
Best of all, you don't have to replace your strap to use Wandrd's system. If you have a strap you love—maybe a fancy leather strap someone gifted you—Wandrd is selling a DIY kit ($29) that lets you attach its Magnetic CoreLock system to the ends of your preferred strap. Otherwise, the strap kit comes in a 30-mm size ($69), a 15-mm “Lite" ($49), and a wrist strap ($39).
I don't know if Wandrd's system will see the same success as Peak Design's Anchor Links, but I don't see myself switching back anytime soon. Magnets are just too dang cool.
Comments
Back to top

articles.title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
articles.text:
Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.
Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
Suno is facing two more lawsuits over AI music clones.
In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of
cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.
Later in the complaint, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”
Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir Media, and more.

articles.title: Unfold CEO on freeing enterprise data trapped for AI
articles.text:
As enterprises accelerate AI adoption, a major obstacle remains: much of the data AI needs is still trapped inside legacy systems, proprietary software, and applications that lack modern interfaces. Traditional integration tools have helped connect enterprise systems, but they often cannot access the full scope of information or capture the business context needed to make that data useful.
For Ran Cherniavsky, CEO and Co-Founder of Unfold, the solution is to rethink how enterprises access their data. Unfold works through the interfaces businesses already use, extracting information and mapping the underlying logic without requiring system replacements or disruptive migrations.
In this Q&A, Cherniavsky discusses why data accessibility is becoming a defining challenge for enterprise AI, how Unfold unlocks information from otherwise closed systems, and what becomes possible when AI agents can finally understand the full picture of an organization’s operations.
The enterprise data problem
1. Why do so many enterprises still struggle to access critical data trapped inside closed systems, despite years of investment in integration technology?
Because integration was built for systems, not for AI. It connected system A to system B, one field at a time, through whatever the vendor chose to expose. AI needs access to everything a human being can see in a system, and an understanding of what it means. And it needs it fast, without a project for every field. That’s a different problem.
2. What are the biggest risks and business costs of leaving data locked inside systems that lack APIs or other standard interfaces?
Companies that can’t put AI on their core data will fall behind the ones that can, and that gap opens fast.
The costs show up long before that. Companies pay specialized consultants, year after year, to map a system’s fields by hand. Analysts pull capped reports manually and stitch them together in Excel. AI pilots stall because the model only sees the slice the API exposes, and gets the answers wrong. In effect, you’re renting access to your own data through someone else’s UI.
And there’s a risk you can’t see: if nobody can read what’s inside a system, nobody can be confident it’s secure either. You’re left hoping.
3. Between security, IT modernization, and AI adoption, where does inaccessible enterprise data create the biggest problem today, and why?
AI adoption, and it’s not close. That’s where the pressure from the board is, and that’s where locked data costs you right now. You can’t just open Claude and ask, “A dealership owner can’t ask Claude how old the warranty money owed to him is, because that data is stuck behind reports?” Not because you can’t write the question in plain English, but because the data isn’t accessible.
Security and modernization feel the same problem, but differently. Security is a symptom: you can’t secure what you can’t see. Modernization is the long way around. According to Gartner, 45% of core systems still run on mainframes or on-prem client/server, and 34% of organizations now leave core applications as they are because modernizing them is too risky. AI can’t wait for that to change.
Solve access and context for AI, and you’ve solved a big part of the other two along the way.
Unfold’s technology and differentiation
4. How does Unfold access systems that have no APIs, exports, or open interfaces?
The same way a person does. Employees don’t work with a system only through its API. They use the UI, reports, exports, files and more. Unfold works through every interface the application exposes, with or without an API.
Our team spent years doing deep software research, integrating with systems regardless of what they exposed. That used to take months per system, by hand. With AI, Unfold becomes the subject-matter expert on a system in days, maps where every piece of data lives and how it moves, and then builds a deterministic read-only collector that gets it out through the system’s own permissions.
That works on mainframes like AS/400, on-prem ERPs, and modern SaaS that only exposes part of its data. If a system has a UI or a command line, we can work with it. Onboarding takes up to 14 days, for any system.
5. How does Unfold understand the context behind a system’s data, rather than simply extracting the raw data?
Raw data without meaning is noise. In Oracle’s ERP JD Edwards, tables carry numbers instead of names. A status field holds a code nobody remembers defining. Two systems call the same customer by different names.
Unfold learns each system the way a trained employee would: what each object means, how objects relate, which business rules and exceptions apply, and how people actually use it. Because we see the screen and what sits underneath it, we can tie what a user sees in the UI to where it lives in the data.
That knowledge used to live with SMEs, implementation partners and vendors, and much of it walked out the door. We rebuild it as a catalog of every data object, with its business meaning and its full journey through the system. AI gets the data and the context together, and stops guessing.
6. How do you ensure that data from different enterprise systems is normalized, governed, and ready for AI applications?
Once each system is understood, we connect them. The same customer is KUNNR in SAP and an Account in Salesforce. The same site has a different ID in each ERP. Unfold maps all of it into one canonical enterprise schema, so data from every system arrives normalized and consistent.
Governance is built in from the start. The data stays with the customer, in their own source systems. Lineage comes with it, because we know where every field came from and how it was transformed.
And the collectors are deterministic: the same question returns the same data every time. That’s what you need before you let an agent act on it.
7. How does Unfold complement existing platforms like Splunk, Snowflake, and Databricks, and what makes its approach different from traditional integration tools?
First, we don’t replace data platforms; we feed them. Splunk, Snowflake and Databricks are where data gets searched, analyzed and put to work by AI, and they’re only as good as what reaches them. Today, that’s whatever a source system’s API or export allows. And you don’t have to move the data at all: Unfold can work with it where it lives, in the source systems, or deliver it straight to agents through our connector to Claude, Gemini and others.
Unfold sits upstream. We get the data and the logic out of the systems that never fed those platforms, with the meaning attached, and deliver it wherever the customer needs it: their lake, their warehouse or their agents. At a global retailer, point-of-sale data from an AS/400 mainframe is heading into a Gemini Enterprise fraud-detection agent. At a manufacturer, plant control system data is heading into a CMDB.
Traditional integration starts from a catalog of prebuilt connectors and moves what each vendor exposes, one project at a time. Unfold starts from the system itself: every interface, the full data model and the business context, in days rather than months.
Customer applications and business impact
8. What are the most compelling real-world use cases for Unfold, and how do customers measure the value of unlocking previously inaccessible data?
The best use cases start the same way: someone sees data in a screen and can’t get it into the workflow they need. A few examples:
A global retailer needs point-of-sale data from AS/400 systems in more than ten countries feeding its fraud detection, which now runs on Gemini Enterprise. One country’s regulator told them to stop selling until that control was in place.
A top-10 US insurer pays contractors with specialized expertise to map claims-system fields to the database by hand. Then another team of engineers comes in to build the ETL. All of that takes weeks. We do it automatically, in days.
A multi-store auto dealership group had its parts, service and warranty data locked behind reports in its dealership management system.
Now the owner asks, in plain English, “How old is the warranty money owed to us?”
Customers measure value in three ways: time (days instead of months), cost (consultants, professional services and engineering they no longer need), and outcomes that weren’t possible before, like an answer across systems, or a business that keeps selling.
9. How does Unfold help enterprises modernize legacy infrastructure without disrupting critical operations or replacing existing systems?
By not touching them. Unfold doesn’t require code changes or a migration. It works with the system as it is, through the interfaces that are already there, and read only, by design.
That matters because modernizing core systems is risky, and everyone knows it. Gartner finds that 34% of organizations now leave core applications as they are for exactly that reason, up from 16% in 2023, and that 40% of the modernizations needed for autonomous business will be late by 2030.
So instead of waiting years for a replacement, you get the data and the business logic out today and put AI to work on top of it. And when you modernize, you already have a full map of what the old system holds and what it means, which is a big part of the migration work.
10. What new capabilities become possible when AI agents can access and understand data from previously closed enterprise systems?
AI adoption stops crawling and starts running. Today, enterprises work for AI: teams spend months on integrations just to feed it data. Once every system is open and understood, that flips. We work with AI, and AI does the integrations and runs the workflows itself.
Agents stop guessing and start working on the real business. Most agents today reach email, documents and a few SaaS APIs. The core of the business, the orders, claims, inventory, warranty and plant operations, lives elsewhere.
Open that up, and a dealership owner asks one question across parts, service and warranty. A fraud model sees point-of-sale data from every country. A finance team gets on-time-in-full numbers across two ERPs that use different IDs for the same site.
Then it compounds. Agents follow a process end to end, like order-to-cash, across every system it touches, instead of stopping at the edge of one. That’s when AI moves from answering questions to running the business.
The future of enterprise AI
11. Will data accessibility become one of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption, and how can organizations overcome it?
It already is. Gartner says that through 2030, the biggest compounding challenge for agentic AI is data access and control. Models keep getting smarter, but more intelligence alone won’t move the enterprise. Models need the enterprise’s proprietary data, and the context of how each system is used.
How to overcome it: start from the business outcome, not from a data project. Pick one AI initiative that’s blocked by a system you can’t get data out of, solve it, and expand system by system on the same layer. Stop treating access as a string of one-off integrations, and don’t wait for modernization to finish.
And treat the knowledge inside your systems as an asset. The people who understood those systems are retiring or gone. Capturing that context now is part of being AI-ready.
12. How do you see the enterprise integration market evolving over the next three to five years, and what role do you expect Unfold to play?
History tends to follow the same path. First we invent something. Then we find a commercial way to use it. Only years later does it actually change how we live. The first modern car came in 1886, but it took decades to transform society.
That time went into building the infrastructure around it: roads, gas stations, bridges. AI is at that same point today. We have probably the most powerful engine we’ve ever built, and the models keep getting better. But the transformation inside enterprises hasn’t happened yet, and the reason isn’t intelligence. The roads aren’t there.
Integration is a big part of those roads, and it was built for a different kind of traffic. It connected systems to systems with connectors and pipes, moving one field at a time. Over the next three to five years, the traffic changes. AI is now the one that needs the data, and AI needs all of it, along with what it means.
So I think the market splits. Moving data becomes a commodity, like a basic road. The value moves to the layer that understands the enterprise: full access to every system, the business context behind it, and one schema across all of them.
Gartner already treats AI context platforms as a separate market, growing from $28B in 2026 to $78B by 2030. It also notes that these platforms are limited by how much they can actually get out of systems of record. That’s exactly the gap we fill.
The difference this time is that we don’t have to wait 40 years. With AI, enterprises can build the roads much faster than they built them for the car, but only if their data can actually reach the engine. Our goal is to lead this category and become the knowledge foundation for enterprise AI, so that every AI use case in the enterprise runs on Unfold, from the mainframe to SaaS.
The founder’s vision
13. What inspired you to build Unfold, and what is your long-term vision for the company?
Our team spent years doing deep software research, getting data out of systems that were never designed to give it up. Then AI arrived, and suddenly every company had the same problem we’d been solving by hand, at a scale nobody could staff. Twenty years ago, your data sat on your own servers.
Today it sits behind vendors, interfaces, and knowledge that’s retiring. We built Unfold so AI can understand any enterprise system the way a long-time employee does. The long-term vision is simple: every AI use case in the enterprise runs on Unfold, from the mainframe to SaaS.
