articles.title: UK has no plans to slow down AI data center construction - Engadget
articles.text:
UK has no plans to slow down AI data center construction
The country’s growth minister said the data centers will continue as “essential infrastructure” projects.
As the US deals with the fallout associated with the ongoing demand for data centers, the UK is looking to capitalize on it instead, according to one of the country's ministers. Dan Tomlinson, the UK's minister for growth, told the The Financial Times that data center construction will continue as "essential infrastructure."
Tomlinson told FT that AI is becoming more widely used throughout the UK's economy, meaning the country will need more data centers to support that growth. However, the minister added that data center construction in the UK will have to invest in local communities and create jobs to receive government support. Tomlinson also told FT that the UK government has taken away some lessons from the "free-for-all in parts of the US" with data center construction and that the country would take a more nuanced approach with better oversight.
According to the UK Compute Roadmap, a policy paper detailing how the country can meet AI's growing power demands, the UK needs to have at least a computing capacity of 6GW from data centers by 2030. The UK previously made it easier for data centers to earn approvals, thanks to the "AI Growth Zones" initiative introduced by former prime minister Keir Starmer in 2025. However, UK residents have taken to protesting on sites of planned data center construction. Across the Atlantic, a majority of American voters said they're in favor of restricting the rapid pace of data center construction in local ballot results.

articles.title: Building a smart home across different brands? Here's what you should know - Engadget
articles.text:
Building a smart home across different brands? Here's what you should know
Getting all of your devices to talk to each other doesn't have to be hard.
On paper, the easiest way to build a smart home is to pick a single brand with a broad range of accessories, and stick with it. That greatly simplifies setup and control, not to mention potential choice paralysis, given the sheer number of accessories out there. And really, simplicity is the whole point of smart home technology.
In practice, however, an omnibrand approach is usually impossible. Most companies specialize in a single product category, or a handful of them at most. The company that manufactures a smart lamp probably isn't going to produce robot vacuums too. In any event, sticking to a single brand means you're out of luck if a competing product delivers better features or pricing.
The smart home industry has been aware of these concerns for a long time, which is why there are now quite a variety of hardware and software platforms intended to make multi-brand systems work, from Amazon Alexa through to Zigbee. Here's what you need to consider when setting up your own.
What you need to know about multi-brand smart homes
The easiest solution to this is choosing one of three major smart home platforms: Amazon Alexa, Google Home and Apple Home (and therefore HomeKit). They're designed with multi-brand pairing in mind, so all you have to do, typically, is make sure the appropriate "Works With" label is on the box, and follow platform-specific pairing instructions. We say "typically" only because there might be unrelated requirements, such as support for a specific wireless standard.
There are alternatives. One of the most popular among enthusiasts is Home Assistant, since it's open-source, and can unite other multi-brand platforms under one gigantic umbrella. It is aimed at more tech-savvy users, however. You can buy a premade Home Assistant hub, but if concepts like installing your own hub on a Raspberry Pi sounds a little intimidating, you might be better off sticking with the big three.
One important technology that that's breaking down barriers is Matter. This is a universal pairing protocol, meaning that if an accessory supports it, you can link it to any of the platforms we've just mentioned. There are a few catches, mind. First, you'll need a device on your platform that's marked as a Matter controller, most often a hub, smart speaker or smart display. Second, pairing through Matter often limits an accessory to generic functionality (as I've discovered), rather than the full feature set from a specific to a brand or platform. Lastly, not all product categories are available, though most of the essential ones are — from light bulbs through to EV chargers.
Other important factors to be ready for
Another consideration is wireless technology. Hubs (and hub-like devices) based around mesh protocols like Zigbee, Z-Wave and Thread can potentially unite accessories from multiple brands. If a hub lacks Matter-based pairing, however, it may be unable to pair accessories from other brands, despite the fact that these protocols are supposed to be industry-wide standards. The perennial example of this is the Philips Hue Bridge, which can only pair select third-party Zigbee bulbs, and even then doesn't grant them every feature. If wireless pairing flexibility is essential to you, you may end up having to switch to a hub-centric platform, such as Home Assistant or Homey.
When selecting any platform, it's vital to think about the devices you want to control things from. While Alexa, Google Home and others have apps for both iOS and Android, HomeKit is exclusive to Apple devices. You may also prefer the interface(s) for one platform over another. It's usually possible to pair accessories with two or more platforms, with or without Matter — but unless you're really into tech, it's far simpler to pick one and stick with it.
Don't forget to consider the quality and quantity of accessories a platform supports. Alexa and Google Home are by far the best supported, giving you more options when shopping, with HomeKit ranking a distant third. If you're really into the idea of Apple's HomeView display, however, or pairing HomePods with your Apple TV 4K, you can probably make do with the limited selection of third-party HomeKit products.

articles.title: How to Remind Your Boss of Your PTO Without Pissing Them Off
articles.text:
You're about to slam that laptop shut for two weeks when the boss messages, “See you Monday!”
We've all been there, staring down a manager who has forgotten about our paid time off—even though we told them!
When we communicate something that's important to us, we can forget that it's not necessarily as meaningful to the recipient. Surely you've been on the flip side, too, annoyed at a coworker who hasn't replied to your messages, until someone mentions that they're on holiday.
A key to efficient communication in the workplace is to repeat yourself. It sounds counterintuitive, but it's true. We're all better off when we overcommunicate by saying the same thing two or three times.
The trick is how and when you do it. Think of all the avenues you have for requesting, recording, and reminding people of your PTO. Use all the channels, and spread out the messaging so that each instance has relevant context and timing.
6 Weeks to 6 Months Out: Get It on the Books
If you like to plan in advance, you might request time off four to six months out. Not all managers appreciate this much notice, however, because they might not know what the workload will be when your vacation rolls around, making it hard for them to approve your dates.
How far in advance you should request time off is a conversation to have with your direct boss. It depends on them as a person, the type of work you do, the size of your team, and other factors. If this conversation doesn't give you much clarity, four to six weeks before your time off is probably about right. Start there and adjust as necessary.
Occasionally, you need approval well in advance for an event that cannot move and will cost you a lot of money to cancel, like your own wedding or a nonrefundable trip. In those cases, six months or more is not unreasonable, but bring it up from time to time so no one forgets.
Whenever you put in your initial request, it must be recorded. Log it into a time-off system if your organization uses one (human resources software, a shared calendar) or write it in an email with a clear subject line, and make sure your boss replies saying it's approved.
2 Weeks Out: Verbal Reminders
About two weeks before your time off, remind your boss and colleagues verbally in meetings. The ideal settings are in a weekly one-on-one meeting with your direct manager and in a team meeting.
Save your info for the end of the meeting after all pressing business has been discussed. If you need to make sure your responsibilities are covered while you're out, raise that point privately with your manager rather than in a team meeting so the boss has time to decide how to handle it.
1 Week Out: Email or Message Your Contacts
If you need to tell someone beyond your team—such as clients or another department—about your planned time off, do so in writing a week before you leave. This gives them plenty of opportunity to reach out while you’re still available.
Email is fine, though if you usually communicate with these people through Slack or Microsoft Teams, that may be a better option. How you format the message matters—see the next step for tips.
2 Business Days Out: Send Formatted Messages
Two business days before your time off begins, send a short, clear message to everyone who needs to know that you will be out. If the norm is to use Slack or Microsoft Teams, use that.
How you format this message makes a huge difference. The first sentence should say something like, "Just a reminder, I will be out beginning DATE. I will be back on DATE." This sentence can be in bold. The second DATE is the day you return to work, not the last day of your PTO. What's relevant to your colleagues is the day you are available.
If you need to give more information, such as who is covering for you, put that in a new paragraph. Do not go overboard with detail. It will make people crazy. Should you need to leave detailed instructions, put them in a shared document and link to it.
Why send this message two business days out? Simple: If your first PTO day is Monday, you send this message on Thursday so that anybody who takes off or calls in sick on Friday still sees it in time.
The Day You Leave: Set Your Status
My favorite PTO reminder is the status indicator in a team messaging platform. Set it to show you're out and add an appropriate emoji, like a palm tree or airplane.
Even if you dislike emoji, they are extremely efficient and effective communicators here. At a glance, everyone who sees it is reminded that you're out.
You can typically set a status message too; use this to tell everyone the date you’ll be available again.
Your First Day Off: A Final Reminder for the Extra Forgetful
For those supremely forgetful bosses and coworkers, you might set up an automated message that appears at 8:30 am the first day you're out. Slack, Teams, email, or even a text message will do the trick. Be concise. Be kind. And have a sense of humor. The point of the message is to be helpful—not make someone else feel like a forgetful jerk.

articles.title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
articles.text:
The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.
Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
You can get a temporary break from the $200 price hike that hit both Air sizes this summer.
If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.
Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5)
Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.
If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

articles.title: Anthropic buys $3.4bn of gas generators, FT reports
articles.text:
The deal covers 1.7 gigawatts of large generators, the FT said, citing one person who knows about it. Anthropic signed it in late September with OnePWR Solutions, a power supplier in San Antonio, Texas. TNW has not independently confirmed the deal.
OnePWR had ordered the generators from Caterpillar about two years ago but needed money to complete the purchase, the FT reported. Anthropic first planned to buy power from OnePWR. Instead, it took over the orders, plus the work needed to install the machines.
Anthropic did not buy OnePWR itself, and none of its staff moved to Anthropic, according to the FT. It is not known where the generators will be used.
Both companies declined to comment to the FT. They also did not immediately respond to Bloomberg, which followed up the report.
The deal comes as Anthropic prepares for its stock market listing. Its amended IPO filing last week showed $895bn in commitments, almost all for computing power and infrastructure.
Other AI firms have also used gas to get data centres running fast. Elon Musk’s xAI faces a lawsuit over gas turbines at its Memphis site.

articles.title: A 55-Year-Old Math Problem Was Solved—This Time by Humans
articles.text:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
The late Ronald Graham wore two hats. He was a renowned mathematician and, at one time, president of the American Mathematical Society. He was also a serious juggler and president of the International Jugglers’ Association. “He loved tricks,” said Fan Chung, a mathematician at UC San Diego who was married to Graham. “You know, spinning a ball, spinning a coat hanger, spinning several balls together, throwing pens against the wall.”
Sometimes Graham wore both hats at once. “It’s interesting, in fact, that many mathematicians and computer scientists have an interest in juggling,” he said in a 1980 television interview. “I think it’s the search for patterns and structure that is responsible for this.”
He would go on to write numerous papers, some with Chung, on the mathematics of juggling. But back in 1971, decades before he made that connection explicit, he posed a question that some mathematicians now say might have been inspired by juggling, too.
Start with a random set of different integers, not including zero. Can you always rearrange them so that if you add up the first two numbers, then the first three, then the first four, and so on, every “partial sum” turns out different? In the language of juggling, this would mean that if each ball stays in the air for a different amount of time, you can always find an order to throw them in such that two balls won’t come crashing down on the same beat—which would ruin the act.
If the numbers are all positive, then the answer to Graham’s question is obviously yes: The sums will always grow larger as you add more numbers. Similarly, if there are both positive and negative numbers in the mix, the answer is also known to be yes. But what if the numbers live in a finite world—like numbers wrapped around a clock, which repeat after a certain count?
That’s what Graham wanted to know. He conjectured that the answer should still be yes. It often happens, he figured, that even when dealing with rigid constraints, you can still find enough flexibility to construct special patterns or structures—just as it’s usually possible to find a valid sudoku board or Latin square (another kind of puzzle) despite their many rules. “It fits nicely in all these questions about designs and about very symmetric structures,” said Noga Alon, a mathematician at Princeton University. But for decades, no one could prove Graham’s intuition to be true.
That changed recently, when several young mathematicians picked up the balls. In a proof that spanned four papers and various fields of mathematics, they finally resolved Graham’s rearrangement conjecture. The final paper, by Lisa Sauermann of the University of Bonn and Huy Tuan Pham of the University of Chicago, appeared in February 2026, officially closing the problem.
Across the papers, one theme prevailed: the power of randomness to draw out patterns. As Alon put it, “It’s the power of collaboration, the power of the young generation, the power of probabilistic methods” that solved the problem.
Alp Müyesser, a mathematician at the University of Oxford, often finds himself drawn to problems whose solutions need two ingredients: a random process and something extra as well. After solving one such problem in 2022 while he was still a graduate student, he encountered Graham’s conjecture and realized that his just-finished proof could help there, too.
The conjecture is set in the world of clock arithmetic. You start by placing the whole numbers on a number line, then you wrap the line around the face of a clock so that the numbers repeat after some prime number, p. Say p is 7, for instance. In this setting, 0, 7, 14, and all other multiples of 7 are equivalent—meaning that you can add two positive numbers (like 3 and 4) and get zero.
Graham asked the following: If you pick any set of nonzero numbers off this number line (for any p), can you always rearrange them so that the partial sums you get are all different?
The challenge depends on how big your set is compared to p. The more numbers you pick, the more sums there are to manage. But if you choose fewer numbers, there will be fewer ways to rearrange them. These different cases inspire different approaches.
Müyesser, along with his former adviser, Alexey Pokrovskiy of University College London, tackled the case where your set includes almost every possible number up to p. With sets this large, it can be extremely hard to construct a valid ordering. But it turned out that starting with a random ordering can bring you most of the way there.
“Computer scientists often call this a ‘finding the hay in the haystack’ problem,” Müyesser said. You might know that lots of good orderings are out there, but actually finding one is hard. “If you do it randomly, it’s likely going to work, but it’s hard to explicitly describe what the solution is supposed to look like.”
Müyesser and Pokrovskiy needed to ensure that no sequence of numbers anywhere in the ordering added up to zero. Otherwise, adding those numbers to the previous partial sum would repeat that sum.
A completely random ordering might have a few of these troublesome sequences. So Müyesser and Pokrovskiy first set aside a few specially chosen numbers from the set, then randomly scrambled the rest. They scanned their random ordering for any problems; if they came across an interval that added up to zero, they could insert one of the spare numbers to change it. In 2022, they posted their solution, though it was hidden in a paper that focused on applying the same technique to a more general problem.
A couple of years later, Noah Kravitz of Oxford, unaware of Müyesser and Pokrovskiy’s solution, stumbled on Graham’s conjecture in an online archive of unsolved problems. “I saw there was an open problem, and I was like, it’s embarrassing for humanity that we don’t know this,” Kravitz said. “This situation just had to be rectified.”
He decided to approach the conjecture from the opposite end. Together with Benjamin Bedert of Oxford, he considered the case where the set of numbers is tiny compared to p—for instance, Alon said, if you have a set of 100 numbers where p is 1 billion.
Kravitz and Bedert solved Graham’s conjecture for those cases and posted their proof in September 2024. Müyesser saw it and reached out, sharing his own work; the three of them (plus two other colleagues) then teamed up to extend Müyesser’s original approach.
“It was a pretty unlikely combination of people,” Kravitz said. He and Müyesser come from two areas of combinatorics that don’t typically collaborate. “Different sections have completely different techniques,” he said.
Their paper, which they posted in August 2025, handled more cases where the set of numbers is relatively large compared to p. But between those cases and the small-set cases that Kravitz and Bedert had covered, a gap remained. No one could figure out what to do about medium-size sets, such as those that include roughly half as many numbers as p. “Our methods didn’t work there, and there were clear reasons that they would not have worked,” Müyesser said.
It seemed as though research on the problem might enter another long hiatus. Then, in February 2026, a surprise appeared online.
Lisa Sauermann and Huy Tuan Pham were old friends. The two mathematicians had met in 2015 at Stanford University, where Sauermann was a graduate student and Pham an undergraduate. Today they live on different continents—Sauermann in Bonn, Germany, and Pham in Chicago. But a conference in Germany in September 2025 provided a rare chance for them to share a chalkboard again, and afterward Pham followed Sauermann to Bonn for a short visit. All they needed was a problem to work on.
At the conference, they heard two talks on Graham’s conjecture by mathematicians who had attempted but failed to bridge the gap. They were intrigued. And as it later turned out, Sauermann had encountered a closely related problem in the International Mathematical Olympiad as a high school student. She solved it correctly, and by the time she finished high school, she’d won a gold medal in the prestigious competition four times. (Most likely, it was Chung who placed the problem on that year’s exam, as she was on the committee that wrote the questions, and she frequently took inspiration from Graham’s many puzzles.)
By the end of their three-day visit, Sauermann and Pham had a plan for how to crack the case.
It hinged on a technically demanding method called anti-concentration. Here, an anti-concentration statement asserts that some event has a particularly low chance of happening. But the mechanics of proving these kinds of statements are so intricate that, though Kravitz and others were aware that such an anti-concentration approach might succeed, “we just hadn’t had the guts to actually try it,” he said.
First, though, Sauermann and Pham began the way their predecessors had. They randomly reordered their set of numbers and came up with a procedure to fix any problems—that is, any sequences that add up to zero. Any time they found a zero-sum sequence, they swapped out the last number in the sequence with another one.
This procedure often went without a hitch. But three types of “bad events” would cause it to fail. One: A zero-sum sequence might occur toward the end of the entire arrangement; then there would be no other numbers to swap in. Two: Many zero-sum sequences might appear too close together, making it impossible to fix them all. And three: Fixing one bad sequence might create another zero-sum sequence down the line.
Sauermann and Pham hoped to prove, using anti-concentration, that each of these bad events was sufficiently unlikely. Then there would have to be a way to rearrange the set of numbers to satisfy the conjecture.
To do this, the duo used Fourier analysis—an area of math that lets you rewrite functions as sums of simple waves—to show that in general, when you add up random sets of numbers, no one sum is especially likely to appear. They then used this insight to carefully estimate the probability that each bad event would occur, ultimately showing that the total chance of getting a bad event was less than 100 percent. That was enough to settle the conjecture.
A few months after their stint in Germany, Sauermann and Pham posted their 27-page proof online. They had shown not only that a satisfactory rearrangement was always possible, but that a random ordering could be rearranged to eliminate bad events at least 90% of the time—a massive success rate.
The mathematicians who had previously worked on the problem were surprised to see the remaining case closed so quickly. “Their approach is just completely different,” Müyesser said.
Together, the four papers prove Graham’s conjecture for sets of all sizes. But they all assume that p is very large; though no one has calculated its exact value, think along the lines of 10 raised to the 100th power. To mathematicians, that’s fine—the salient point is that you’re working in the setting of clock arithmetic. But another aspect of the problem technically remains unsolved—you might still try to resolve the conjecture for all p. And if you want to use the result to choreograph a real juggling routine, you’re out of luck: To correspond to such a large p, the routine would have to be much too long.
The proof confirms that even within these strange, limited number settings, “there are some nice structures that always exist,” Alon said. You can always achieve some degree of flexibility, shuffling the numbers in your set around to avoid revisiting the same partial sums.
“To pose a good problem is really an art,” Chung said. “I think Ron would be extremely happy to see the problem solved.”
Original story reprinted with permission from Quanta Magazine, an editorially independent publication of the Simons Foundation whose mission is to enhance public understanding of science by covering research developments and trends in mathematics and the physical and life sciences.

articles.title: US Justice Department sets up AI task force
articles.text:
The US Justice Department has set up a task force to lead its work on AI crimes and AI lawsuits. It is called the Super Intelligence Task Force, the department said on Thursday.
The name follows a September order from President Donald Trump telling federal agencies to call AI “super intelligence” in official documents.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will lead the group. It will go after foreign states, criminal gangs, and people or firms that use AI for fraud, the DOJ said.
The task force will also absorb the DOJ’s AI Litigation Task Force, according to an internal memo from Attorney General Todd Blanche dated 13 October, Nextgov reported. That unit was created in January to challenge state AI laws in federal court.
The new group will also set priorities and write rules for how to prosecute AI crimes, according to Nextgov. It will be the DOJ’s main link to the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, led by intelligence director Jay Clayton.
“The Department of Justice will continue identifying and prosecuting individuals whose use of SI violates the law,” Blanche said in a statement.
Weiss said the DOJ would also push firms to keep tight controls so their AI works as planned. The DOJ did not say how many staff the task force will have or what it will cost.

articles.title: The pros and cons of using your laptop with the lid closed - Engadget
articles.text:
The pros and cons of using your laptop with the lid closed
Will it damage your laptop over time?
Laptops have come a long way since they became popular in the mid-to-late 2000s. Back then, they were bulky and heavy, with very short battery life. They were also seen as a lesser version of the desktop, with weaker hardware and limited capabilities. Today's laptops are much thinner and lighter, their battery life is far better, and their hardware can go toe to toe with most standard tower PCs.
For that reason, many people now buy a laptop as their main computer and connect it to a regular monitor, keyboard and mouse. Some like to keep the laptop open and use its screen as a second display. Many others prefer to leave the lid closed.
So which approach is better? What are the pros and cons of using your laptop with the lid closed?
Reasons to keep your laptop lid closed
Let's start with the bottom line: There's no huge advantage or disadvantage to keeping your laptop open or closed. There are a few small differences, but at the end of the day it's mostly an aesthetic choice. Some people just like the clean look of a desk with nothing on it but the essentials: keyboard, mouse, cup of coffee. The laptop is tucked away and doesn't add to the clutter.
A few small advantages come with that, and they can help your laptop last longer and stay looking new. There's the regular wear and tear of opening and closing the lid, for one. The keyboard stays clean and protected inside the closed lid and, above all, dust doesn't pile up on the screen, the laptop's surface and between the keys.
With the screen off, the laptop also draws much less power, and you don't have a second panel lighting up the room when you're working late.
Reasons to keep your laptop lid open
Other people prefer the look of a workstation with two, sometimes three, screens. Keeping the laptop open next to a bigger monitor gives you extra screen space for things you want in view, like a second browser window, a music player or, these days, an always-on AI assistant working away in the background while you keep one eye on it.
Open also usually means better heat management. Many laptops push heat out through the keyboard area, and an open lid lets it escape. It matters most on gaming laptops, which run hot. PCWorld notes that some, like the Razer Blade 16, vent air out of the top of the keyboard. Some laptops are also designed to lift up off the desk when the screen opens, which gets a lot more air moving across the parts that heat up.
Which to choose, and how to do it right
Which one should you pick? It depends on the laptop and on what you ask of it. A fanless MacBook Air or any thin, low-power machine is fine closed all day, and you can even buy stands made for exactly that. If you're running a gaming laptop or any workstation that gets properly hot, leave it open. And if you're unsure, check the manufacturer's site to see whether it's happy running under load with the lid shut.
If you go closed, there are a few things worth doing. Keep the power adapter plugged in, since the laptop draws more power with an external monitor attached, and you don't want the battery draining quietly in the background. In Windows, open Control Panel and look for Choose what closing the lid does, then set both lid options to Do nothing, or the laptop will go to sleep the second you shut it. Put it on a stand so air can get under it, and don't count on a cooling pad to do much; those only lower temperatures a little and don't cool the gap between the screen and the body.
There's also a middle road. Close the lid just far enough to switch the screen off, but not all the way, and as long as hot air isn't blowing straight onto the display, it should be fine indefinitely. It won't keep the dust out, though, so plan on cleaning the laptop every so often.
Overnight jobs are the easy case. A render, a big download or an old laptop acting as a home server can all run with the lid shut, as long as the vents are clear and the work is light to medium. Heavy loads are another story.
If you keep it open, the tips are simpler. Give the laptop some space so the air can move, keep the vents clear and, if it's a gaming laptop, tilt it up on a stand.
One tip works for both approaches: Get a docking station. A good one takes the keyboard, mouse, network cable, HDMI and audio out, so the laptop only needs one cable to connect to all of it. When you want to take the laptop somewhere, you unplug that one cable and go, instead of pulling five. Most also hold the laptop tilted, so there's room for air to get around it.

articles.title: There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the pressures of creating content for the internet, follow Mia Sato. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
How it started
Almost exactly a decade ago, the media industry was in the middle of a video revolution — or so it thought. In the mid-2010s, publications poured money into burgeoning social media video efforts, chasing the promise of reaching larger audiences and opening new lines of revenue. Print publications and digital news outlets alike hired teams, pumped out content, and entrusted platforms like Facebook with their reach and distribution.
That pivot-to-video slowly revealed itself to be a lot of smoke and mirrors when it became clear that Facebook had inflated video views. Newsrooms cut writers and editors in a move to video — and then cut those video teams when they realized the pivot had not paid off. For many in the media industry, social video brings to mind layoffs and instability rather than the promised abundance.
A “pivot” feels inadequate to describe the current emphasis on social video, not just in newsrooms but in society writ large. Social media companies have reorganized their feeds to emphasize video, spurred by the massive growth of TikTok during the pandemic. But the media industry is still playing catch-up, and in some cases it seems to have been slow to jump in (perhaps cautious given past experience). It took years for some publishers to start incorporating vertical video on their websites, apps, and stories, for example, and it takes coordination and intention to get individual reporters in front of a camera to talk about their work. In the meantime, YouTube has become the most popular streamer, commanding nearly 16 percent of TV viewing, according to Nielsen. Twenty percent of Americans regularly get news from TikTok, and that number jumps to 39 percent for people 18 to 29 years old, Pew found.
Viewers favor the stripped-down selfie-style video dispatches from personalities they trust, even if those creators are not themselves reporting and writing the news. Compared with a decade ago, the barrier to entry and cost of making video content has plummeted: Anyone with a smartphone can become a video creator, no fancy equipment or editing needed. Social video is fast, personality-driven, casual, and, at times, unfiltered — the exact opposite from what news outlets are used to. A second pivot-to-video is underway, and the media industry once again wants in.
How it’s going
Video is unavoidable on social media, if not an expected part of how people and institutions show up online. TikTok’s influence is felt everywhere: on competitor platforms like Meta’s Reels and YouTube Shorts, of course, but also in unexpected places, like LinkedIn. There are no signs of it slowing down, either: The time spent watching Reels on Facebook was at an all-time high in Q3. Early tests in other countries suggest Meta is toying with the idea of dropping users directly into full-screen video upon opening the Instagram and Facebook apps. The appetite for video seems insatiable, and if news organizations won’t lean in, armies of content creators will be happy to scoop up the audiences.
Some news outlets were relatively early to the short-form social video boom. The Washington Post, for example, found notable success on TikTok before many peers had even created dedicated accounts on the platform. (Dave Jorgenson, the face of the Post’s social video effort, left the paper last year. He now makes short and longform videos under Local News International — perhaps a testament to the trust that viewers place in individual creators.)
Beyond having a short-form video presence, some traditional news outlets are leaning into formats and styles popularized in the vertical video era. CNN partnered with Jubilee, the popular channel that produces debate-me-style videos on hot-button political topics. The CNN town hall with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico was conducted in the Jubilee style. The New York Times, which for years has produced polished documentary-style videos, recently introduced the vertical video series “The Call.” Unlike the Times’ more buttoned-up videos, the point of “The Call” is to create a sense of intimacy, like you’re getting updates from a friend: The show’s host ostensibly makes a video call to a journalist reporting on the ground to ask them about what they’re witnessing.
News outlets are also directly hiring or working with content creators. Some outlets like The Washington Post have spun up so-called creator networks, where they partner with influencers to produce content independent from the newsroom. A new program supported by Poynter and Microsoft pairs content creators with a handful of news outlets so they can create content tailored for social media.
And then, of course, there are the clips. Podcasts became videos, which became bite-sized clips of podcasts formatted for vertical feeds. TV shows became web shows, which gave rise to microdramas. News articles — even major investigations — are now adapted for vertical video audiences. Individual reporters (myself included) make talking-head clips explaining our reporting. Earlier this year, I called this phenomenon “the clippening”: the reformatting of all media to be legible in a vertical video feed, even if the original work is neither vertical nor video. It’s hard to fault the people and institutions putting resources into social video — audiences are consuming it — but it’s also feeling a lot like the past.
One of the misguided beliefs of pivot-to-video 1.0 was that traction, views, or engagement on social media platforms would be enough to offset (and ideally surpass) the cost of making the content. For many, that ended up not being true, with flawed metrics, of course, being part of the reason: Virality feels nice, but monetizing that attention isn’t always straightforward. These days, social media companies have largely coalesced around the “views” measurement meaning the number of times a post was served up on somebody’s feed, whether they watched the whole thing or swiped away immediately. How many people who watch a clip of a podcast go on to listen to the full episode? Are the people watching my TikToks about my stories actually going to The Verge to read it, or buying a subscription to support my work? You can’t eat views.
The hope is that we will find new audiences where they’re already spending time. There are millions of people discussing news that journalists are uncovering — it’s important that we reach them, build trust, and be part of the conversation. What’s certain is that if reporters and news outlets don’t, a whole slew of creators will be there to take their place.
What happens next
Just as we’re getting used to short form, the ground is once again shifting under our feet. Not content simply being social media, platforms are looking to be a destination for longer form, higher production quality entertainment. Tech companies know that people watch videos on their phones, but they would also really like users to watch on their televisions, too.
This spring, YouTube’s pitch to content creators (and advertisers) was to make exclusive shows for the platform. YouTube is dominating the TV streaming wars, but other platforms like Instagram are pushing in that direction, too: Its recently announced “Features” effort allows for 90-minute horizontal video uploads, and it seems to be specifically angling for television viewing. (Unsurprisingly, there are a lot of questions from creators about what they get in return for posting longer content.) Some news outlets are already thinking ahead and eyeing longform. The BBC struck a deal with YouTube in early 2026 to create special programming specifically for the platform, then followed it up by announcing a 24/7 YouTube livestream in an effort to reach young people.
Short form isn’t going anywhere, at least right now. But these efforts to move into longer, more resource-intensive video content could be a harbinger of what’s to come — and what could soon be asked of news publishers and influencers alike. News media have had a complicated relationship with tech platforms. On one hand, it’s where audiences are, and platforms allow publishers to reach those people. On the other hand, tech companies signal to outlets (and creators) what kind of content they should prioritize, and everyone has to scramble to meet the new demand. Just as soon as journalists start getting comfortable with front-facing selfie videos, we may be facing a whole new beast: videos that are horizontal and longer, with a higher production value and higher barrier to entry that we typically associate with TV and streaming.
By the way
- Instagram is already starting to place horizontal videos in discovery feeds — I recently saw the format bumped to the top of my Explore tab, mixed in with photos and vertical Reels.
- Even platforms like X that are traditionally associated with text-based content are trying to sweeten the deal to get users to post more videos. The company has an invite-only bonus program that pays creators who post videos regularly. Screenshots shared by X staff indicate that creators can make thousands of dollars for posting vertical videos under 3 minutes.
- If you feel like you’ve been seeing a lot more New York Times Cooking videos, it’s not your imagination: It’s a deliberate strategy to make video content from non-news verticals at the company.
Read (or watch) this
- It would only be appropriate to include a video here, given the topic this week. Here’s Instagram head Adam Mosseri trying to explain the about-face the platform is doing around longform video. The comments on YouTube hammer home a big question: Instagram benefits from more content like this, but what’s in it for creators (and, by extension, news outlets)?
- Short-form audiences were recently described as “rented attention” in the Link In Bio newsletter. Could longer-form content create more durable, lasting relationships between creator (or news org) and audience? Longer formats could put pressure on creators to deliver higher-quality, more in-depth material that is harder to fake than in a quick-hit 60-second clip.
- News publishers are in a constant push and pull with the platforms that make their work discoverable — and not just with social media. Consider Google’s AMP page format, for example, which promised to make the mobile web a better experience for readers. This quote, from my colleague David Pierce’s 2023 story about AMP, really sums up the relationship:
  - “If Google said, ‘you must have your homepage colored bright pink on Tuesdays to be the result in Google,’ everybody would do it, because that’s what they need to do to survive,” says Terence Eden, a web standards expert and a former member of the Google AMP Advisory Committee.

articles.title: UK may add Vinted and eBay to under-16 social media ban
articles.text:
Her comments followed a report in the Sunday Times that the ban would be widened to include the two resale sites. The paper said the concern was that messaging tools let strangers groom children. It said Depop and Facebook Marketplace could also be added.
However, the change would go further than the original plan. When the government announced the ban in June, it said it did not intend to include e-commerce platforms.
Both eBay and Vinted already say users must be at least 18, according to the BBC. eBay told the BBC that the details of the proposal were not yet clear, and that it would keep working with the government. Vinted did not respond to the BBC.
The ban will cover sites whose main purpose is social interaction and that let users post content. Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube are among them. The government has not yet published a full list.
Meanwhile, Ofcom set out last month four ways to check users’ ages, including photo ID and facial age estimation. A similar ban took effect in Australia last year, where many children have got around it.

articles.title: The reason why some USB ports are teal - Engadget
articles.text:
The reason why some USB ports are teal
Did you know that different colors have different meanings?
It's a fairly normal thing to look at the different slots and pieces of your computer, knowing full well what most of them do, but being somewhat confused about what one particular element is for. Not everyone can be a super genius, after all, so there's no reason to feel bad about not knowing the reason something is the way it is.
When it comes to ports on your computer, the multitude of different USB slots can sometimes feel strange to look at, considering many of them have different colors. If you have a higher-end motherboard or case, you may also have a lot of them to look at, which makes determining their exact purpose something of a mystery.
After decades of evolution, USB ports have become one of the most versatile ports you can find on your PC or laptop. When it comes to the teal port, it actually has some fascinating use cases, and we'll be breaking down exactly what that color does, as well as how you can use it to your advantage.
What is the teal USB port for?
If you see a teal USB port on your device, you may be interested to know that the color is generally designated for USB 3.1, Gen 2 or above. After its introduction in 2013, USB 3.1 was standardized by the USB-IF, the USB Implementers Forum, with a focus on high transfer speeds and increased power output to devices connected to it. The color isn't a rule, of course, and there are a lot of 3.1 Gen 2 USB ports that have different colors.
While the higher speeds, which can reach upward of 10 Gbps, are a fantastic feature, they're also usually backward compatible with USB 3.0 and prior. You won't necessarily get the same speed benefits, but as USB is one of the most standard ports in computers, you will be able to use most previous generations of USB-A devices with it without issue.
Though it has a distinct advantage over a lot of other USB port colors, there are certain red USB ports that feature USB 3.2. The USB 3.2 ports can reach a top-end speed of 20 Gbps, and though teal-colored versions do exist, they're a bit more uncommon. If you're unsure of the exact possible speed, you can use the Device Manager on Windows or System Report on macOS.
The benefits of using teal USB ports
If you have a teal USB port and can take advantage of its blazing transfer speeds, you may be able to get some spectacular usage out of it. For one thing, the high speed and power output means it can help immensely with any task you need to throw at it.
It's incredibly helpful if you're someone who does a lot of file transfers, or maybe you have a library of games you want to move around to different SSDs. Considering how well USB 3.1 works with high-speed external SSDs, you will be able to significantly cut down any transfer time that may have been slower in the past. This would also help with something like music or content creation, as sample libraries that normally take a long time to move onto SSDs or large video files can be done in minutes.
As teal USB ports tend to favor 3.1 Gen 2, the power output is also a huge benefit. While charging your phone or tablet on your computer's USB ports has usually worked, the power output has generally made it less than desirable. 3.1 Gen 2 is considerably more powerful and can charge things like phones, tablets, earbuds and other smaller electronics with no problem.

articles.title: The MacBook Pro M5 Isn’t Apple’s Newest Laptop, but It’s the Best to Buy Right Now
articles.text:
Last month, Apple refreshed the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the latest M6 chip. It's powerful, has great battery life, and the mini-LED screen is bright. There are all kinds of great attributes about this laptop, but you probably shouldn't buy it. At least, not right now.
While the updated M6 is a perfectly capable laptop in its own right, it fits a bit awkwardly into the current lineup of MacBooks. It's identical to the previous-gen M5 model, which came out in late 2025. But here's the problem: Despite having the exact same laptop specs (save for the chip difference), you can currently get the M5 for $200 less on Amazon and Walmart.
If you're thinking that upgrading from the M5 to the M6 must be worth $200, I'm not so sure. The M6 comes with two additional CPU and GPU cores, which is the origin of most of its gains. While that's not nothing, it's one of the smaller gen-over-gen Apple Silicon performance bumps in the past six years. The main difference is in AI performance, thanks to the second 16-core Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth on the M6. In day-to-day work—or even in content creation workflows—I just don't think the difference will be very noticeable between the two models. That's especially true since the base 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't a true pro laptop in terms of performance. It uses the same M5 chip that's in the MacBook Air and iPad Pro, after all. The only other real difference is in wireless connectivity, where you get the bump to Wi-Fi 7 with the M6 model.
If you're going to buy the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5, though, you should also be considering the 15-inch MacBook Air. The main difference between these two laptops is the quality of the display. The mini-LED panel on the MacBook Pro is much brighter and more colorful, allowing for some very impressive HDR performance. It also has more ports, such as HDMI and an SD card slot. My favorite small feature is its USB-C ports on both sides of the laptop, allowing for charging from either direction.
The 15-inch MacBook Air is actually on sale today, too. The model with 16 GB of memory and a terabyte of storage is at its lowest price since June: $1,549. That's $150 off Apple's retail price.
So, whether you opt for the thinner 15-inch MacBook Air M5 or the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5 with its better screen, you have great deals to enjoy. The same just can't be said as of now for the M6 MacBook Pro.

articles.title: Sola Security builds a context layer for AI security agents
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence is changing how enterprise security teams operate. Tasks that once required analysts to spend hours investigating alerts, correlating data, and navigating different security platforms are increasingly being delegated to AI copilots and autonomous agents.
Yet as organizations accelerate adoption, a fundamental question remains: how effectively can an AI agent protect an environment it does not fully understand?
Enterprise networks are complex ecosystems spanning cloud infrastructure, endpoints, identity systems, SaaS applications, and interconnected security products. The information needed to understand them is scattered across technical platforms, internal documentation, policies, incident reports, and operational workflows.
For AI to become genuinely useful in cybersecurity, access to data alone is not enough. It needs the context to understand how everything connects.
This is the challenge Sola Security is addressing. The company is building what it calls an enterprise security brain: a unified, vendor-agnostic context layer designed to give security teams and AI agents a shared understanding of their entire environment.
Why AI agents still struggle with cybersecurity
The development of large language models and autonomous agents has created expectations that security operations could become substantially more automated. However, applying these technologies to enterprise environments introduces challenges that go beyond the capabilities of individual models.
Ron Peled, Co-Founder and COO of Sola Security, believes the industry’s biggest misconception is that intelligence alone is enough to make AI effective in cybersecurity.
“LLMs are good with text, coding agents are amazing with code, but security isn’t just text and definitely not just source code,” Peled explains. “Security is about relationships, dependencies, connections, and much more.”
The difficulty starts with fragmented information. Security teams must interpret data from numerous products while accounting for organizational knowledge that rarely exists within those platforms. Documents, policies, procedures, contracts, reports, and tickets all contribute to understanding an organization’s security posture, yet AI agents frequently operate without access to this context.
Even centralized data lakes and security information and event management (SIEM) platforms can provide incomplete or noisy representations of the environment. Meanwhile, individual security vendors are introducing their own copilots and agents, each working with a limited view of the organization’s infrastructure. As Peled explains, “They only see a part of it.”
Consequently, even sophisticated AI systems can struggle to produce reliable answers when they cannot connect information across the broader enterprise.
Building a shared security brain
Sola’s approach is to address this context problem at the infrastructure level. Rather than introducing another isolated security product, the company is developing a unified layer that connects information across an organization’s existing tools and systems.
The platform functions as a vendor-agnostic enterprise security brain, bringing together technical information and organizational knowledge to create a continuously maintained understanding of the environment. Security teams and AI agents can then consume this validated intelligence through their existing workflows.
Sola’s differentiator lies in combining organizational context, security research, and the pre-computation of high-priority intelligence. Rather than waiting for a question or an agent request, the platform continuously identifies and prepares the most relevant information, making it available proactively or on demand, wherever and whenever security teams need it.
Importantly, organizations do not need to replace their current security infrastructure to adopt Sola. The platform is designed to work with existing products and data sources, connecting information that would otherwise remain fragmented across different systems.
Its coverage spans cloud environments, endpoints, identity systems, SaaS applications, and coding agents. By understanding individual entities alongside their relationships and dependencies, Sola aims to answer complex security questions that would otherwise require analysts to investigate multiple platforms and manually correlate findings.
Consistency, governance, and cost efficiency
A shared understanding of the enterprise also has implications for how organizations govern and scale AI deployments. When different agents independently retrieve and interpret information, their answers can vary depending on which systems they access. Sola instead aims to provide a consistent intelligence foundation, with answers grounded in evidence from across the environment.
Its architecture also addresses the security implications of autonomous systems. Rather than giving multiple homegrown agents their own production credentials, organizations can use Sola as a governed, read-only intelligence layer. This provides AI systems with the context they need without unnecessarily expanding their operational permissions.
There is also an economic consideration. Repeatedly asking AI models to explore systems, retrieve information, and reconstruct organizational context consumes tokens and analyst hours. Sola says its approach can reduce AI queries by approximately 70% by building and maintaining context centrally, rather than recreating it for every request. The company also positions this model as a way to avoid staffing a dedicated context-engineering team.
Testing the future of autonomous security
Beyond its platform, Sola is investing in research around how AI agents perform in realistic enterprise security conditions. Through its research initiatives and Open.Security, the company examines how agents reason, where they fail, and whether their outputs can be trusted.
This addresses an increasingly important question for security leaders: as more responsibilities move from human analysts to autonomous systems, how can organizations establish confidence in the decisions those systems make? Understanding an agent’s capabilities is only part of the equation; understanding its limitations and the evidence behind its conclusions is equally important.
For Peled and the Sola team, the underlying principle is straightforward. “No matter how smart or powerful the AI model is, without your unique organisational context and knowledge, it will keep struggling, draining time, budget, or both,” he says.
As enterprises move toward increasingly autonomous security operations, the next competitive advantage may not come exclusively from deploying more powerful models or adding more agents. It may come from the infrastructure that allows those systems to understand the organization as a whole. Sola Security is building around that premise, positioning the enterprise security brain as a foundational layer for the agentic era.

articles.title: 5 unexpected uses for your old smartwatch - Engadget
articles.text:
5 unexpected uses for your old smartwatch
Breath new life into your old tech with these handy tips.
Upgrading to one of the best smartwatches can be exciting, but it often means your old smartwatch is left with nothing to do. Unfortunately, it's at this point that users may toss their old smartwatch in a drawer and forget about it. But it doesn't have to be like that.
Your old smartwatch is a versatile piece of hardware, so despite how it seems, that small device that's been gathering dust still has some pretty unexpected and interesting uses. With the right guidance, you can give your old smartwatch a new lease on life, or at the very least, you could sell it for some quick cash. Even if your smartwatch no longer receives major OS updates, you can still use it as a dedicated AI tool, an easy-access note-taking device, a child monitoring tool, or a dedicated sleep tracker. So free your old smartwatch from its drawer and blow the dust off. Most of these unexpected uses only take a few minutes to set up and require an extra app or two, though some require a cellular plan or a phone for full functionality.
Use your old smartwatch as a dedicated AI voice assistant
If you use AI tools like Gemini or ChatGPT, one of the more relevant uses for your old smartwatch is to turn it into a dedicated AI assistant device. Setting things up is pretty simple, allowing you to get answers from or talk to your AI, all without having to pull out your phone. On Wear OS smartwatches, Gemini is the primary option. While on the Apple Watch, Siri is the default — but you don't have to stick with Siri.
On watches running Wear OS 4 or later, you'll need to first make sure Gemini is installed and has been updated. Once that's sorted and voice activation is enabled, all you need to do is say "Hey Google," and Gemini will respond. If voice activation isn't your style, you can alternatively press and hold the side button to activate Gemini. On Samsung watches, you'll need to customize the side button so it can activate Gemini. To reassign, open Settings > Button and gestures > Double press > scroll to where you see Gemini and select it.
On the Apple Watch, activating Siri is straightforward; simply raise your wrist and say "Hey Siri" or press and hold the Digital Crown. You can use the Wrist AI app to gain ChatGPT or Gemini functionality, but the free tier only allows a small number of chats daily. For easier access, you can add a Wrist AI complication to your watch face. For Wear OS watches, to get ChatGPT going, you'll need the WristAssist app, but it's been removed from the Play Store, so you will have to sideload it. You'll also need an API key from OpenAI to get things going; creating the key is free, but usage is billed.
Turn your old smartwatch to a quick note taker
A good use case for your old smartwatch is simply making it a note-taking device thanks to more accurate AI transcriptions. So instead of having to pull out your phone from your pocket every time you get an idea or want to jot down some thoughts, you can raise your wrist and speak.
Your old smartwatch likely already has a note or voice recorder app, so what you need is preinstalled. On Apple Watch, you can say "Hey Siri," then "Record a voice memo" to get started.
You can get transcriptions of the notes recorded on both Wear OS watches and Apple Watch, but you'll need your phone. On Samsung watches, you can get transcriptions in the voice recorder app using the built-in speech-to-text mode, but it has a 10-minute limit. Recordings taken on your smartwatch should automatically sync across your devices, so a note you recorded during your morning walk should be waiting on your phone by the time you get home.
Use your old smartwatch to track your sleep
There are few things as important to the human body as sleep, and your old smartwatch can help you improve it. But you'll have to sacrifice charging your watch overnight, potentially leaving you with a drained battery in the morning. And that's precisely where your old watch comes in. You can charge it all day, then wear it to bed while your main smartwatch charges.
Setup usually takes just a few minutes. To track your sleep and view your sleep data on Apple Watch, set up Sleep in the Health app on your iPhone, then turn on the Track Sleep with Apple Watch setting. For a Galaxy Watch, connect the watch to your phone, then open the Sleep tile on your Galaxy Watch and follow the prompts to get it set up. Keep in mind that how well this works and how much data it can track depends on the model of your smartwatch, because they don't all offer the same sensors, especially older models.
Lastly, don't treat the reported numbers with the same weight as a diagnosis from your doctor, because sensors can be inaccurate. So, if you notice anything concerning in your sleep report, take it as a cue to talk to your doctor, not as a diagnosis.
Your old smartwatch can monitor your child
Your old smartwatch can find a new purpose on your child's wrist as a dedicated kids' watch. When set up, your kids can call, text, and share locations without owning a smartphone. Do note that this only works on LTE/Cellular smartwatches, and a smartphone isn't needed for the child after configuration.
Samsung watches have a dedicated Kids mode that gives parents plenty of oversight over their child's experience. So apart from the usual location monitoring, calls, and texts, parents can also approve or block apps, set School Time limits, and use Google Family Link to manage the child's watch usage. Unfortunately, Kids mode isn't available on every Samsung Watch; you'll need an LTE Galaxy Watch 6 and above.
Apple Watch offers a similar feature called Apple Watch for Your Kids, and it's supported on Series 4 or later with cellular, or an SE with cellular on watchOS 7 or later. As you'd expect, it can make calls and send texts, has location tracking, screen time management, and Schooltime mode, which, like Samsung's equivalent, is basically restricted so the child doesn't get distracted during school hours.
Keep in mind that cellular features require a carrier plan, which means additional fees for you. And carrier support varies, so some carriers may not support standalone calling from a smartwatch.
Sell your old watch for cash
If none of the uses work for you, or you'd just prefer to get rid of your device, then your best option is to sell your old smartwatch. It probably still holds some resale value; it's only a matter of finding the right place (or way) to sell it. There are two main routes to go with.
First, you can sell on marketplaces like eBay. Selling on a marketplace may give you the highest payout, but it also comes with the most hassles. You'll have to handle everything concerning the sale, including writing an accurate listing, taking clear pictures, setting a good price, answering questions from window shoppers, shipping it, and then calculating how much platform fees cost you.
Selling to a buyback company like Greenbuyback is the second option that will likely net you less than a marketplace, but it can be more convenient. Simply get a quote online, then ship your old smartwatch to the buyer. Once it's received, it'll be inspected, and if the condition you described matches, you get paid. If it doesn't, you can receive a revised offer. How long the whole process takes depends on the specific program; some pay in as little as 24 business hours after receiving your watch, while others can take up to five business days.
If you don't mind getting store credit and less value for your old smartwatch, then you can trade in your old smartwatch to retailers like Best Buy or manufacturer programs like Apple Trade In. Before you sell or trade in your old smartwatch, make sure to unpair it from your phone and wipe it. On an Apple Watch, unpairing erases it. On Wear OS, sign out of your accounts and factory reset it.

articles.title: World Models Will Soon Be Inescapable. Here’s What You Need to Know
articles.text:
It’s 2016, and you’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk. On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection in Pokémon Go. You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters. What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day help robots navigate obstacles and interact with objects.
Niantic, the creator of Pokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models. “We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon, Niantic Spatial’s chief technology officer. He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas. Unlike the text-based nature of large language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.
This software is poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models. 2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics and driverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models. It’s time to better understand how these bots think.
“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO of Odyssey, an AI lab focused on world models. “With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds. “They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.
McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments. He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.
It’s not just humanoid robots that could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models. Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.
“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist at Wayve, which builds world models designed for cars.
Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage. The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.
Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games. Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players like Tencent are investing in their own world models.
You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements. Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology. Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raised over a billion dollars recently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup. Additionally, famed Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li launched a startup in 2024 called World Labs, which AMD acquired this year for over $8 billion.
Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes. To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it. Earlier this year, I strapped an iPhone to my forehead and recorded hours of videos in my apartment. I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout. As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.
Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life. Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass. I’m sorry I didn’t tidy up first.
