articles.title: Stock futures rise slightly as investors eye AI trade, brace for more data and earnings: Live updates
articles.text:
Stock futures were slightly higher Sunday evening with traders eyeing whether technology shares can continue to recover, while they are awaiting the release of key inflation data and earnings from major AI companies this week.
S&P 500 futures gained 0.1%, while the Nasdaq 100's added 0.3%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 101 points, or 0.2%. 
Over in Asia, markets were mixed on Monday, with South Korean equities continuing their sharp selloff from Friday.
The benchmark Kospi index fell marginally, while the small-cap Kosdaq index declined 0.87%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.39%, after initially starting the day in positive territory.
Japanese markets rose, however. The Nikkei 225 gained 1.97% and the Topix climbed 2.8%.
Later Monday, investors will look to inflation data out of China, with economists polled by Reuters expecting a reading of 0.8%, down slightly from September's 0.9%.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal AI-driven selloff, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite bounced 1.09% to 24,579.42 and the broad-market S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86. The blue-chip Dow, however, lost 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to settle at 51,285.73.
Broader investor sentiment remained cautious following a batch of stronger-than-expected jobs data. Additionally, concerns linger after the Democrats' strong midterm results, amid fears that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom.
The tech sector will also be focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. A proxy for Nvidia shares was lower by 2% over the last 24 hours in trading on Hyperliquid.
Liz Ann Sonders, Schwab Center for Financial Research chief investment strategist, noted that the Nasdaq and Nasdaq-100 are oversold, with heavy de-risking by traders. Thursday marked the biggest day of retail selling since the Covid pandemic, according to Vanda Research. Retail traders haven't been taking advantage of the selloff, Sonders said.
"Retail has not proven to be the dip buyers that they have been in the past," she told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Friday. "You saw a really heavy amount of net selling … we may not fully be washed out yet, but we'll have to see whether that retail trader at some point decides to step back in."
Sonders suggested that the next short-term focus should be on companies' adjustments to capex plans and expectations for future profit margins.
This week, investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave, Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent selloff has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
On Monday, traders will get September wholesale inventories data at 10 a.m. ET. Take-Two Interactive Software, Occidental Petroleum, KKR, Constellation Energy and Skydance are scheduled to report quarterly earnings.

articles.title: Read Huang's email to his staff and statement from Nvidia's board of directors
articles.text:
Nvidia on Sunday said it has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies said is a Chinese spy.
"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement.
Below is a staff email from Huang obtained by CNBC and a statement released Sunday about the investigation from Nvidia's board of directors.
Staff email from Huang:
[From:] Jensen Huang
[To:] Employees
Subj.: A message to our company
Nov. 8, 2026
To my colleagues at NVIDIA,
I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.
Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.
Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.
— Jensen
Statement from Nvidia's board of directors:
The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.
While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.
Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.

articles.title: Trump says renewed Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ if talks progress but warns he could still strike
articles.text:
President Donald Trump said he is "highly unlikely" to restart open war with Iran, but warned he could still strike the country as Washington tries to reach a deal with Tehran to end the conflict.
The now more than eight-month-old war, which stoked inflation and sent oil prices surging, has seen repeated bursts of fighting separated by ceasefires and peace talks for months. It was widely speculated that Trump might restart open conflict after the midterm elections, where his Republican Party lost badly to Democrats.
Trump's comments came during an interview with CNN, where he said restarting the war is unlikely as long as talks to constrain Iran's nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz make progress.
"It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump said. "The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary. They're a failing nation."
Trump, however, left the door open for additional strikes if he deems it necessary. The president reiterated his threats to strike bridges and power plants in Iran if the war restarts.
"I've got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They're fully locked and loaded," the president said. "We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour."
An end to the war and reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would likely ease oil prices, though finding a truce has proven difficult. All previous attempts to end the war and reopen the strait have been met with disappointment.
Trump is likely to come under increased pressure to end the conflict, however, now that Democrats have won control of both the House and the Senate. Some Republicans are also likely to be eager for an end to the war, given the role high gas prices played in their drubbing at the ballot box.
The president has demanded Iran fully open the Strait of Hormuz and agree to never develop a nuclear weapon as part of any deal.
Later in the day on Truth Social, Trump posted that "Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran."
"Coupled with history's greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!" he said.
Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, describing it as an initiative aimed at "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."
The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports for months.

articles.title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy
articles.text:
Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times.
Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry."
An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.
In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement.
Read Huang's email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors' statement here.
The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security.
The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models.
Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
Nvidia's Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout.
In his note to staff, Huang said he was "proud and grateful" to be an American.
Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18.
Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.

articles.title: Democrats amp up Trump investigation threats, Blanche counters he may probe lawmakers
articles.text:
Top Democrats are ramping up oversight of the Trump administration and businesses it has partnered with, while Attorney General Todd Blanche warned he could counterinvestigate lawmakers conducting probes.
Democrats romped to majorities in both the House and the Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, putting them in position to seize control of committee gavels and subpoena power in January. The electoral rout leaves Democrats with at least 54 Senate seats and 254 seats in the House of Representatives as votes continue to be counted in several states.
Democrats vowed to investigate both President Donald Trump's White House and businesses that have worked with the administration. CNBC reported on Thursday that Democrats are expected to take an aggressive approach to probing businesses, especially those companies with ties to the Trump family. The technology, cryptocurrency and prediction market industries, among others, could immediately be in the crosshairs.
"If you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations — serious ones," said Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, on CBS' "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "The American people are just damn sick of this."
Blanche, Trump's former personal attorney, whom the Senate narrowly confirmed as the nation's top cop earlier this year, took umbrage at the Democrats' plans for investigations and said he may launch his own investigations against members of Congress.
"There could be," Blanche said Sunday when pressed on CNN's "State of the Union" about whether the administration will counterinvestigate Democrats.
"When the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration because somebody will come after them, at some point you have to draw the line."
Blanche was referring to comments made by Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who said during a University of Chicago event that she wants "young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?'...I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. And so let me avoid participating in that.' I want that deterrence message sent."
Trump has ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats over the comments.
Blanche also took aim at Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee — appearing to caution lawmakers who sit on the panel. Garcia warned the administration and business leaders to "lawyer up" after the election.
"I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee," Blanche said.
Garcia shot back, saying on CNN: "What Todd Blanche is doing right now is a threat."
"He's trying to stop us from doing real oversight," Garcia said. "He is the person that should be reading the Constitution, because the Constitution makes it very clear that it's our job in Congress to conduct oversight of the executive and the administration."

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces bipartisan congressional scrutiny over reported China spy link
articles.text:
Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for congressional investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions.
In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement.
"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement.
Lawmakers have been calling for an investigation into the relationship and are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about it.
"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers."
Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January.
Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang.
Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times.
Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported.
Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks.
Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X.
Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang.
Neither Nvidia nor the Commerce Department immediately responded to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.title: Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
articles.text: There's one question on everybody's mind entering the new trading week: Where are artificial intelligence stocks going next? The engine of the four-year-old bull market is coming off a bruising week , sparked by the midterm elections, when gubernatorial candidates who support restrictions on data center development won big in states like Texas and Ohio. Voters across the country also approved local ballot measures that could slow the pace of AI investment and construction. As Jim Cramer made clear at Friday's Annual Meeting , this is a real risk to the future earnings of chipmakers, electrical equipment suppliers and other companies with brimming order books to support the AI buildout. We take it seriously and may need to make further adjustments to our stock portfolio to reduce AI exposure. This headwind didn't blow in from nowhere. It's why we exited Corning in early September and Broadcom in late October , and two months ago initiated positions in the non-tech stocks of Kimberly-Clark and Bank of New York . The upshot after such a whirlwind week for the market? No Club holdings are reporting in the coming days and the economic calendar is also fairly light. Here's a closer look at what to expect: 1. AI earnings: Neocloud CoreWeave's earnings report on Tuesday night will help determine whether the AI trade can regain momentum. Even before the election, we've been paying close attention to CoreWeave's bonds and stock as a barometer for souring investor appetite for AI names. How the market responds to CoreWeave's results and commentary on the conference call could have far-reaching implications. "That's going to be the one," Jim said at the Annual Meeting. "You either believe [CEO Michael Intrator] and you see the stock go up and you realize that the AI trade is on. Or you don't believe Michael and the stock plummets, and it'll be a really bad day. ... CoreWeave is so important. It's insanely important." On Thursday morning, CoreWeave's peer in the neocloud game, Nebius , delivers earnings of its own. And that evening, networking giant Cisco Systems and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials will release quarterly results. Both companies are also cogs in the AI trade, so they're firmly on our radar alongside CoreWeave and Nebius. 2. Inflation and Fed speakers: Inflation — and the Federal Reserve's response to it — will also be front and center this week. The October consumer price index is due out Tuesday morning, followed by the producer price index on Friday. As of Sunday, traders are pricing in 78% odds for a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool . Hot inflation data will likely prompt the market to price in additional tightening ahead, especially in light of an October jobs report on Friday that illustrated the resilience of the U.S. economy. In addition, a number of central bankers are set to give public remarks throughout the week, and their speeches carry market-moving potential of their own. Consider what happened in the runup to the Fed's October meeting, when New York Fed President John Williams said on Sept. 29 that he saw "no need for urgency" on another hike. The market had been pricing hikes at both the October and December meetings, but that shifted to just one additional hike after Williams' comments hit the tape. So, we need to pay attention to both the inflation reports and all the Fedspeak coming our way. Among them, we'll hear from Fed Governor Christopher Waller on Tuesday and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday. Both central bankers are voting members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year. articles.title: 'What makes you tick': NWSL, WNBA owner Kara Nortman on a personality test she uses to build success
articles.text:
Business leaders often look back to "aha" moments in their lives for enduring lessons about their success.
For Kara Nortman, who had a long and successful career in technology and venture capital before becoming a women's professional sports owner, that moment arrived when she attended the 2015 Women's World Cup Final in Vancouver.
After watching the U.S. team win, Nortman couldn't find a jersey to buy, or much of any merch, or even information online about women's soccer. And that gap stayed with her as something that suggested an untapped business opportunity. She began researching women's soccer, went on to advise the U.S. women's national team players' union, and ultimately co-founded Angel City Football Club in Los Angeles, the most valuable women's football club in the world, and now majority owned by former Disney CEO Bob Iger and his wife Willow Bay.
But looking back, Nortman says none of that would have occurred without her belief in a personality test called the Enneagram. It helped her understand why following her gut on women's sports and changing her career trajectory felt right. "The Enneagram was a huge unlock for me," she said on the latest episode of the CNBC Changemakers podcast, explaining that she identifies as a Type Seven, which she connects with "discovery, creation [and] adventure."
Nortman says over the course of her career as a team leader, she has tried multiple personality assessment tools, including the DiSC model, the Hogan Assessment System, and Myers-Briggs, but she says that they didn't lead to the kind of change in team dynamics she was looking for.
The Enneagram groups people into nine personality types based on their core motivations. Nortman said the framework not only helped her better understand herself, but also what drives others. While some people are motivated by power, others may be driven by creativity, safety or rules, she said.
That perspective shaped the way Nortman — who also co-founded Monarch Collective, an investment firm focused on women's sports — has approached building teams. In addition to Angel City FC, Monarch is an investor in NWSL teams Boston Legacy FC and San Diego Wave, German Bundesliga team FC Viktoria Berlin, and the WNBA's Cleveland Sirens, set to debut in the 2028 season.
Nortman said that she used the Enneagram with Angel City co-founders Natalie Portman and Julie Uhrman to discuss how they communicated and made decisions. When she launched Monarch Collective with Jasmine Robinson, she said, they used the test with each other and began profiling people who joined the firm.
The point isn't just about identifying someone's "type," according to Nortman.
It's understanding how various personalities affect a team and how to help people work well with each other. Nortman said during the podcast that the Enneagram is "a new lens by which to view yourself and the team."
"I think this idea that we all have to be good at everything is not right," she said. Rather, doing great work involves "knowing how to show up in that environment as a member of the team ... helping bring out the best in others," she added.
Earlier this year at a CNBC Changemakers event, Nortman said the Enneagram also helped her better understand her husband, whom she described as a Type Six, motivated by fear — a "danger ranger," she joked, the person who spots a problem in a company's cash flow early or shows up to a Burning Man camp with a first-aid kit and extra water.
"You want him on your team, you want him in your marriage, and sometimes he's a thorn in your side," Nortman said. Recognizing that, she added, helps her respond with more empathy, and understanding her own personality helped her understand her motivations when drawn to risk and building new things.
"It kind of impacted everything, not just a massive career pivot, but my marriage and even the way I show up as a mom," she said. It is a way to understand "what makes you tick," she said, rather than focusing mainly on how others observe your behavior.
Figure out how to be credible and in a way how to fit in, but really hold onto what makes you different. That is what will change your industry. That is what will change the world.
The nine-point Enneagram system traces its modern development to Bolivian philosopher Oscar Ichazo, and its introduction to the U.S. in the 1970s to figures who studied with Ichazo including psychiatrist Claudio Naranjo and neuroscientist John Lilly, maybe better known for creating the sensory deprivation isolation tank. More extensive adoption of the Enneagram in the U.S. during the 1980s was supported by Enneagram evangelists including Don Richard Riso and Helen Palmer.
Despite the system's popularity, the scientific evidence remains mixed. A systematic review published by the Journal of Clinical Psychology in 2021 of 104 independent samples found "mixed evidence for reliability and validity." Some studies suggested it could help with personal growth, but researchers found that analyses often did not support nine distinct types.
But Nortman is not alone among business leaders who cite use of the Enneagram as a factor in their success.
Dropbox co-founder and co-CEO Drew Houston, who announced his plan earlier this year to step down from day-to-day management in the future, said an Enneagram description helped him recognize how strengths such as creativity could also lead to conflict avoidance and a lack of structure at the company. "At first I was skeptical, but after reading the description for my type I found it spookily accurate in pinpointing what makes me tick: what motivates me, what my natural strengths are, what my blind spots tend to be, and so on. It's helped me tailor my role and leadership style to my strengths," he told Tim Ferriss for the entrepreneur and angel investor's book "Tribe of Mentors."
"It's even better with a team—all of our senior leaders have typed themselves and we encourage everyone at Dropbox to learn about it. ... Over the last few years, I've found myself looking at all my important relationships through the Enneagram lens."
Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke has said Shopify used employees' Enneagram types as a tool for understanding how colleagues might work together. "Enneagram, it has worked very, very well for us. In our internal system, you can actually see the Enneagram with everyone else," he told Ferriss in a 2019 episode of the investor's podcast.
Lütke says it is less important what your personality type is than that you and those around you understand it and how to train it. "And I think this is so fruitful of a discovery, especially early in your career because, again, a lot of the people we hire, the average age at Shopify is 29, I think. So we get to people very early in their career because the thing that we want to accomplish, and this is really the goal of all of the internal programs, is we want to .... find out what kind of areas they have a fixed mindset on, and try to get people to acquire a growth mindset. Think of their intelligence as something that can be trained. Think of their skill as a program and not as something static. ... And once people acquire this growth mindset on at least a number of different traits, usually, they make it very, very far, and they can have 10 years of a career in one year on the work clock."
Nortman's advice is less about fitting into a category and more about understanding what makes people different. "Figure out how to be credible and in a way how to fit in, but really hold onto what makes you different. That is what will change your industry. That is what will change the world," she said during the CNBC Changemakers event earlier this year.
Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title: Recent AI agent experiments reveal a risky future of machine 'teamwork' inside corporations
articles.text:
AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face.
AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work.
In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the "collective."
The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. "Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board's cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their 'peers.' The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents "rarely limited their behavior."
Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization.
And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together.
Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another's mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction.
Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation.
AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts.
For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one.
'Least ethical solutions'
In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as "AI organizations" — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals.
Across 12 tasks that Anthropic gave the AI organizations, one key double-edged finding emerged: the multi-agent organizations were "significantly" more effective at achieving business goals than individual agents, but their solutions were also less aligned with ethical goals than tasks run by single agents.
"AI Organizations both produce solutions that are on average more effective and less ethical but also discover the most effective and least ethical solutions across multiple rollouts," wrote the authors of the study, which was conducted by Anthropic in conjunction with the MATS Program, which studies AI alignment.
The researchers suggested that there is a significant difference between a rogue agent and a rogue team of agents. "Our results demonstrate that organizations of aligned agents may favor trading off ethics for business effectiveness in ways that single agents do not – consequently, intuitions for how single-agent systems make ethical decisions and tradeoffs may not generalize to multi-agent settings," they concluded.
The scenarios in which these tradeoffs may take place are wide-ranging, with the Anthropic researchers citing opening an auto plant, downsizing a company, and manipulating election sentiment as examples.
The problem isn't necessarily that any individual agent has gone rogue. It is that the organization itself can behave differently from its individual members. A single agent may recognize that a proposed action is unethical and it may refuse to take the action. But the research finds that in agent team scenarios, "agents who did not consider ethical implications often ignored emails from agents who did."
Anthropic's research found that in the consulting business scenarios it created, "the perfect ethics score and low business score responses occur when the single agent refuses to generate a proposal or entirely pivots from the proposal requested."
But if some agents in an AI organization refuse to participate in the proposal, other agents who do participate will stop emailing these refusing agents and continue to forward their contributions to other agents who are also participating.
In effect, when an organization divides the job among several agents, each may focus on its assigned piece of the problem rather than the consequences of the whole. That's nothing new for corporations, with misaligned incentives a primary cause of dysfunction among human teams within organizations. But it is an entirely new manifestation of this behavior among the machines.
In its software development agent testing, in which the researchers used a scenario in a life-or-death intensive care unit, single agent solutions tend to prioritize minimizing the percentage of sepsis cases missed, while "most of the lowest cost per patient (highest business goal) solutions were found by the AI Organization – these very same solutions also score the lowest on ethics as measured by cases missed."
Expertise can be lost, AI 'groupthink' emerge
Other early research suggests another failing across AI teams that doesn't relate to ethical boundaries being crossed: failure to recognize who the real expert is.
Unlike human teams, AI teams "consistently fail to match their expert agent's performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is," according to a study conducted by Emory University and Stanford University researchers.
"One important lesson from multi-agent research is that a team of capable AI agents is not necessarily a capable AI agent team," said Hancheng Cao, an assistant professor of information systems and operations management at Emory University's Goizueta Business School.
Groups of AI agents often performed worse than their strongest member, even when they knew which agent was the expert. Rather than taking advantage of the expert's knowledge, agents tended to compromise between expert and non-expert opinions. The researchers found that this tendency toward compromise increased with team size and was associated with poorer performance.
"Collective failures don't necessarily require individual agents to behave badly," Cao, one of the study's authors, said.
That distinction matters for companies considering multi-agent systems. A team can fail even if none of its members is deliberately acting against the group's interests. It may simply combine information poorly, defer to the wrong agent or settle on an answer that is worse than the best answer already available.
In all, the evolving research points to an underlying problem for the effective use of the multi-agent teams: how to strike the right balance in the world of machine teamwork.
Agents built from similar models can make similar mistakes, which can include agreeing too much. That might resemble a kind of AI groupthink, even if AI systems do not have human motivations or social pressures to produce correlated errors. Similar training, instructions and information can be enough.
"The deep insight from our lab's research is that effective collectives require both alignment (common knowledge, shared goals) but also differentiation (only agents who are different from each other have the potential to complement each other)," said Christoph Riedl, a professor of information systems at Northeastern University.
Two identical agents may simply duplicate each other's work. Two agents with very different knowledge or assumptions may struggle to communicate or pursue the same goal. The right balance depends on the task, and the ideal communication structure, which agents can talk to one another, how often and how much, also varies with the problem.
Riedl said these challenge resemble the ones faced by human teams, and one takeaway should be to not expect better outcomes from AI. "Building good multi-agent AI systems is just as hard as building good human teams: they both face the same information processing tradeoff between alignment and differentiation. It won't magically work better with AI," he said.
Agents can pass along incorrect information, misunderstand another agent's output, optimize for their own metrics rather than the organization's larger objective, or complete their assigned task perfectly while making the overall project worse.
Companies may need to decide which agent has authority over which task, what information gets passed between agents, which systems each agent can access and when a human must intervene. They may also need to build mechanisms for disagreement, rather than assuming that more communication or greater agreement will always improve results.
Some business experts say that takes us back to the "human in the loop" that is so often referenced as critical in the adoption of AI by organizations.
"The problems I see are mostly management problems," said Tsedal Neeley, a Harvard Business School professor and founding chair of the HBS AI Academy.

articles.title: Poppi founder still thinks water's boring—her new beverage company is betting consumers feel the same
articles.text:
After selling her first company, prebiotic soda brand Poppi, to PepsiCo for nearly $2 billion in May 2025, Allison Ellsworth finally got to take time off.
"I went to the doctor for the first time in 10 years and started working out," says Ellsworth, 38. The sale, which included a three-year advisory agreement for Ellsworth, gave her more time to focus on her health. She golfed, went on a GLP-1 and spent more time with friends and family, she says.
But just like in Poppi's earliest days, she avoided a fundamental human need: drinking water, she says. So her husband Stephen Ellsworth — Poppi's former CEO, who teased her about never being hydrated — asked a former employee to concoct a hydration beverage that his family would actually drink.
Such was the beginning of Jetty, Ellsworth's second beverage company, which is set to launch Monday. The startup sells bottled drinks and powder packets with electrolytes meant for "normal people," in contrast to hydration products that market toward athletes or people in search of hangover cures, says Ellsworth.
"It's a solution to boring water," says Ellsworth, adding that she wanted something more natural than red-colored sports drinks for her kids after soccer games. "You can drink three of these a day. It's just not that deep."
"I don't feel super sexy holding a Gatorade bottle," she says.
'Are we really doing this again?'
When Ellsworth sipped an early version of Jetty, she looked at her husband, and said, "Are we really doing this again?"
As at Poppi, Ellsworth is Jetty's chief brand officer while her husband serves as CEO. They're familiar with the time and effort necessary to build a new brand. And Jetty is set to enter a smaller market than Poppi ever did: Soda is one of the largest players in the beverage industry, while hydration is newer and more niche. Beverages with a hydration claim brought in $10.5 billion in sales over the last 52 weeks, part of $159 billion in total beverage sales, according Nielsen IQ data.
But starting a second business after successfully exiting another comes with advantages, says Ellsworth. Jetty is immediately launching online at Target and Amazon and nationwide at Whole Foods Market stores, saving about two years' worth of brand building, she says. And with some startup capital already in hand, the Ellsworths can wait to seek out external funding, she notes.
"The pressure is a little bit off of generational legacy and wealth," Ellsworth says. "The best part this time is we get to pick who we work with, what we want to do. There's just so much more control of the chaos this time." But external forces can still wreak havoc.
Competing in a crowded beverage aisle
Jetty, which touts having less sodium and sugar than sports drinks, isn't the first hydration business to sell electrolyte mixes meant for non-athletic use. Nuun, for example, describes its no-sugar electrolyte tablets as a "water enhancer" for "everyday hydration" that users can also drink up to three times per day.
Still, such products don't exactly dominate the drinks aisle at grocery stores. Beverages with hydration claims, half of which are sports drinks, make up about 6% of overall beverage sales, according to Nielsen IQ data. Notably, most people get an appropriate amount of electrolytes — elements like sodium, potassium and magnesium, which the body requires to function — from a healthy diet, the Cleveland Clinic wrote in a September 2023 blog post.
Ellsworth spots opportunity nonetheless, with some American consumers shifting toward "functional beverages" and away from soda, according to an October 2026 report from consultancy EY-Parthenon. Hydration isn't yet a distinct category, like sports or energy drinks, but it feels like the next step in beverage evolution given how much today's consumers prioritize wellness, says Don Johnson, principal in the EY-Parthenon Consumer Strategy practice.
Gen Z also cares a lot about flavor, and young consumers may be more prone to try hydration drinks instead of regular water, says Lokesh Ohri, consumer products sector leader at EY Americas.
Ellsworth says she's confident that Jetty can attract such customers with the type of culture-focused branding that helped elevate Poppi. "People laughed at me when I was like, 'I'm making a better fruit soda,'" she says, referring to her first company. "Now it's like, 'Hold my Jetty.' It doesn't scare me."
But getting consumers to try a new drink is only half the battle for businesses like Jetty, notes Ohri. If a beverage startup wants to build loyalty and longevity, it has to prove to consumers that its product actually improves their lives, he says.
Picking up where Poppi left off
Ellsworth has another reason for starting a beverage company: She's too young to retire, she says.
Instead, she aims to take what she learned from Poppi and apply it to Jetty. With her new startup, the husband-and-wife duo decided to focus on hiring and investing in personnel even before coming up with a business plan, Ellsworth says: "When I brought in people that were better than me [at Poppi], it allowed me to shine at what I was good at, which was the creative, the brand, the digital-first, the culturally relevant stuff."
They're applying other lessons from building Poppi too, says Ellsworth. In April 2025, just before Ellsworth's exit, Poppi settled a class-action lawsuit — which alleged misleading health claims, related to the company's former tagline, "Be gut happy. Be Gut Healthy" — for $9.8 million.
"We were really buttoned up with this product to make sure there's nothing we couldn't say on here that anyone could sue us for," she says, noting that Jetty's branding avoids the word "healthy."

articles.title: Poppi founders are going after PepsiCo's Gatorade with new beverage startup Jetty
articles.text:
After disrupting the soda category with Poppi, founders Allison and Stephen Ellsworth are now taking aim at hydration with their new brand, Jetty.
Starting Monday, Jetty drinks and ready-to-mix electrolyte packets will be on shelves at Whole Foods grocery stores and available online at Target and Amazon.
The new, self-funded venture directly pits the Ellsworths against PepsiCo, which bought Poppi for $1.95 billion in 2025. Pepsi owns Gatorade, which dominates the U.S. sports drink category with about 60% market share, according to Numerator data.
Poppi shook up the soda category with prebiotic fiber, low calorie and sugar counts and its fun marketing aimed at Generation Z and millennials. Jetty looks to upend the hydration category through a similar strategy. To do so, it will face off not only against Gatorade but also a swarm of other upstarts looking to get in on the electrolyte-fueled trend.
For decades, Gatorade and other sports drinks have pitched their products to athletes who need electrolytes and fluids after an intense workout, although many consumers drink them every day without even sweating. Jetty is aimed at people who need a hydration boost, but not the same level of electrolytes or sugar as a traditional sports drink.
"No one has really created a product for just everyday hydration — literally everyday hydration for normal people," Allison Ellsworth, Jetty's chief brand officer, told CNBC. "Like I woke up this morning, I didn't run a marathon."
The GLP-1 hydration dilemma
Following Poppi's sale to PepsiCo, Ellsworth stayed on as an advisor to the brand, although she said she is no longer involved in the day-to-day operations.
After 10 years building Poppi, Ellsworth said, she finally had free time. As Ellsworth tells it, she went to the doctor for the first time in a decade. She started using a GLP-1 medication and lost 60 pounds.
That's how Jetty came to be.
Ellsworth's husband, Stephen, now CEO of the new brand, noticed she wasn't hydrating, even when she came back from the gym.
GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro can make people less thirsty. But because staying hydrated can also help mitigate some of the drugs' side effects, such as nausea and headaches, it can become more important.
"I physically struggle getting liquid into my body," Ellsworth said.
Jetty is meant to solve that problem.
Plain old water is often less appealing to consumers, even dehydrated GLP-1 users, but more flavorful options with added benefits can be tempting. About 44% of GLP-1 users report consuming more functional beverages, according to EY-Parthenon's third annual survey of more than 3,600 current or former GLP-1 users.
Ellsworth sees a broader appeal for Jetty, too.
"Our core audience is going to be millennial moms and Gen Z," she said. "Gen Z just isn't relating to these old school brands, the legacy of the Gatorades and the Powerades. They're just not cool."
Electrolyte elevation
Consumers broadly have become more interested in staying hydrated.
Dollar sales of hydration and electrolyte products climbed 20% to $2.6 billion over the 52 weeks ended Oct. 4, based on data from SPINS, which tracks new universal product codes, or UPCs. The category also has a strong repeat buyer rate of 62%.
However, the Ellsworths aren't the only ones to notice the potential in hydration. The number of new items in the category with annual sales of at least $10,000 has increased 41% over the last two years, according to SPINS.
Big food and beverage companies have been looking to hydration, too.
Kraft Heinz debuted Capri Sun juice pouches and Kool-Aid packets with electrolytes this spring. In April, Pepsi unveiled an overhaul of the Gatorade brand, focused on making it more appealing to a wider swath of consumers, with more potential occasions like a "fresh morning start" or an "afternoon walk." And Electrolit is a top performer for its distributor Keurig Dr Pepper, with 40% retail sales growth in the company's third quarter.
All of that means more competition for shelf space and consumers' "share of throat," an industry term for beverage market share.
To increase Jetty's visibility across the grocery store and to maximize convenience for shoppers, Jetty will be available in both powders and bottles.
Single-use electrolyte mixes are growing at a much faster clip than the ready-to-drink category, Ellsworth said, thanks to Unilever's Liquid I.V. and smaller upstarts like LMNT. On Amazon alone, powders are a $1 billion category, according to Ellsworth.
The ready-to-drink, or RTD, sports beverages are a much larger market, but the category's sales are shrinking as consumers reach for other hydration options instead. Unit sales of sports drinks have fallen 9.1% from 2022 to 2026, according to Numerator data. And Coca-Cola has written down the value of BodyArmor by more than $1.7 billion after buying control of the brand for $5.6 billion in late 2021.
That doesn't worry Jetty's founders.
"Me and my husband know how to do RTD," Ellsworth said.
Jetty will launch with five flavors, including watermelon, orange mango, fruit punch, black raspberry and white cherry. All of them contain 100 milligrams of sodium, 310 milligrams of potassium and 100 milligrams of magnesium in a 15.2-ounce bottle or 15-gram packet.
In addition to electrolytes, Jetty products also contain B vitamins, 3 grams of fiber and 6 grams of sugar. It doesn't use artificial sweeteners or dyes, its founders say.
For comparison, a 20-ounce bottle of traditional Gatorade Thirst Quencher has about 270 milligrams of sodium and 80 milligrams of potassium, plus 34 grams of sugar. The sports drink brand is also phasing out artificial colors and promoting lower-sugar versions.
"What's really interesting about this product and this opportunity is we now can capture all those lapsed drinkers — or that generation that didn't even ever drink it in the first place," Ellsworth said.
Jetty vs. Gatorade
Poppi's new owner knows about Jetty and the market it is trying to capture, too.
"I don't think [Pepsi] gets it, but what they do get is that the movement is changing, and they think that just by taking dyes out or doing 90% less sugar, they're going to capture this audience," Ellsworth said. "But that is very big corporate thinking."
She added that she believes Pepsi has missed the mark on advertising to Gen Z consumers across its portfolio, such as in its campaigns for Sprite competitor Starry.
Perhaps as an extension of that, Poppi's performance has been underwhelming under PepsiCo's ownership.
The food and beverage giant now estimates the fair value of potential performance-based payments to Poppi's prior owners is $12 million, Pepsi said in a regulatory filing in October. At the time of the deal, Pepsi promised an additional payment of $300 million if Poppi hit certain targets by the third quarter of 2027. The Ellsworths declined to comment on the filing to CNBC.
This time around, with one successful brand under their belts, Jetty's founders say they have learned from past mistakes. Those lessons should help Jetty as it launches at a much larger scale than Poppi did.
Three different claims lawyers have signed off on Jetty's packaging, according to Ellsworth. Poppi paid $8.9 million to settle class-action litigation alleging false advertising over its "gut healthy" claims.
For now, Jetty is entirely self-funded with $2.5 million, although Ellsworth said that the brand will likely raise money in 2027. This time, though, she said investors will probably look less like traditional venture capitalists.
"I want to bring in investors that bring value," Ellsworth said. Instead of a venture capitalist who is willing to invest $15 million, Jetty would rather consider investors who can only write a check for $1 million but have access to celebrities. "So then you're getting access to talent on a cheaper level and people that are invested in the brand."
And Jetty has also learned a few lessons from Gatorade. For example, the brand is already at work on a lemon-lime version — the original flavor of Gatorade.
"We'll eventually do it," Ellsworth said. "But it was really important at the beginning just to stick to flavors that we love, for it to taste good."

articles.title: How Democrats will try to end Trump's tariffs
articles.text:
The battle for Congress is over. The war over President Donald Trump's tariffs is about to heat up.
The knotted web of tariffs that Trump spent the last two years weaving could soon face its biggest threat, as Democrats prepare to unload their new legislative firepower against the Republican president's signature policy.
Democrats have made no secret of their plans to bombard Trump and his associates with investigations as soon as the next Congress is sworn in. They are also preparing a first-100-hours legislative blitz, putting forward a series of bills that would unwind much of Trump's agenda.
Both prongs of attack will take aim at Trump's unprecedented use of tariffs, which Democrats have quickly identified as a main target following their landslide victory in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Ending Trump's tariff regime, and especially his trade war against Canada, is something Democrats "absolutely have to do immediately," Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., told MS NOW's "Morning Joe" Thursday.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader who could be elected House speaker in the next Congress, has made clear that ending Trump's tariffs is a top priority.
"We should restore congressional authority as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people," he said at a press conference in late August.
If picked as speaker, Jeffries would speed legislation to the House floor that reasserts congressional authority over trade.
Democrats are also laying the groundwork for investigations into Trump's tariffs, which the party folded into its winning campaign message linking high costs with alleged Trumpworld corruption.
Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, on Oct. 28 asked Trump to hand over records related to tariff exemptions. Trump, Raskin alleges, has wielded the exemption power to cut "sweetheart deals" for industries whose leaders have plied the president with gifts.
The plans are likely to ratchet up the pressure, both legally and politically, that Trump's tariffs were already facing.
The administration is already embroiled in multiple lawsuits challenging different parts of the government's tariff policy.
The most recent suit, filed Oct. 20, targets Trump's use of a Great Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Another court case accuses Trump of trying to recreate the near-global "liberation day" tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in late February. The administration has since been ordered to refund $166 billion in tariff revenue it had collected under the scrapped policy.
Congress, not the president, holds the power to levy taxes under the U.S. Constitution. Over decades, the legislative branch has ceded some of those powers to the executive. But Trump has asserted virtually unchecked tariff powers – which Democrats say they are intent on clawing back.
"Every day Trump insists on his indiscriminate taxes on so many of the products Americans need, he digs a deeper hole for Republicans enabling his tariff spree," said Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is poised to lead the Senate Finance Committee when Democrats take it over.
"If Democrats somehow had a veto-proof majority, or if voters shame Republicans into doing the right thing, there would be no shortage of trade policies to address," Wyden said in a statement to CNBC before Election Day.
"One of the most obvious priorities would be repealing Trump's tariffs on Canada, which are raising prices and harming communities on both sides of the border," he said. "I'll also continue to work to ensure Congress has the final say on tariffs, so future presidents can't reenact Trump's economically disastrous trade taxes."
The Wall Street Journal, citing Wyden, reported Thursday that Democrats are eyeing the Canada trade war as the "first target" in their efforts against his tariff agenda.
Tariff headwinds
As Wyden's statement suggested, the Senate's rules will hamper Democrats' anti-tariff efforts.
Despite their blowout victory Tuesday night, the party will still lack a 60-vote filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, giving Republicans a crucial tool to block legislation even in their diminished state.
Trump is also poised to lean heavily on his veto pen in the next Congress, presenting a major obstacle for Democrats' legislative priorities.
Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate, meaning that even with their historic electoral gains, Democrats would need significant Republican help to force a bill into law over Trump's objection.
Democrats may consider it worthwhile to pass legislation even if Trump vetoes it, as doing so could help them build political narratives in the 2028 election cycle. But they may have other options available.
"Absent the brute force of a veto-proof coalition, Congress might consider other political solutions, such as adding riders on 'must-pass' bills or negotiation with the administration," Kit Johnson, a senior tax manager for BDO's customs and international trade group, told CNBC in an email.
How Trump might respond
Trump has said he plans to use the veto power to force Democrats to the negotiating table. But when it comes to tariffs, it's hard to imagine what deal Trump might accept.
Trump has tried to reshape U.S. trade, foreign and economic policy around his asserted power to slap steep duties on imported goods. He describes tariffs as a win-win, praising them as both a powerful negotiating tool and a major revenue generator.
After Tuesday's election, Trump seemed to suggest tariffs were non-negotiable.
"If I took tariffs off — we have 3,000 plants under construction right now. Every single plant would stop building," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone call Wednesday.
Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has hiked tariffs on nearly every country on the planet, leading to multiple protracted trade wars, most notably against Canada and China. He insists Americans do not share the burden of the duties, even though tariffs by definition are taxes on foreign goods paid by those importing them. The nonprofit Tax Foundation estimates Trump's tariffs have raised the average U.S. household's tax burden by $820 in 2026.
Trump has also consistently overstated the amount of revenue the government has amassed through his tariffs. He claimed before Election Day that tariffs enabled him to offer every U.S. adult $5,000 "dividend" checks if Republicans were to win both chambers of Congress – a plan that would cost roughly $1.2 trillion. But the duties – which are collected from U.S. importers – have only brought in around $300 billion in total between January 2025 and July 2026, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model.
What's more, about $138 billion of that total has been refunded since the Supreme Court ruling in February. Nearly $20 billion in tariff collections are still set to be refunded.
Most voters do not share Trump's rosy view of tariffs. Sixty-five percent of respondents to the CNBC Voter Poll on Nov. 3 said the duties have hurt the U.S. economy, while just 22% say they helped.
What remains to be seen is how hard Republicans in Congress will push back on Democrats' efforts.
A number of GOP lawmakers came out against the duties during the campaign, as their opponents gained ground blaming inflation on Trump's tariffs and the Iran war.
As they try to regroup and look forward to the 2028 election cycle, some Republicans – who largely supported free trade prior to Trump's political rise – may be less willing to continue aligning themselves with Trump's aggressive protectionism.

articles.title: Amazon's Astro home robot has fans but looks destined for the 'trash heap.' Why it's trying again
articles.text:
Jeff Bezos made a bold bet in 2017. A sci-fi and robotics enthusiast, Bezos was convinced that consumers would have a robot in their home in the not-too-distant future.
The Amazon founder and then-CEO told a group of the company's top device executives to get to work on building one, and within a few years, the team came up with the $1,450 Astro.
The public got its first look at Astro, essentially an Alexa-equipped tablet on wheels that can autonomously navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, when it rolled on stage at Amazon's fall 2021 event.
But it never evolved beyond an invite-only product. Astro shipped to just a few thousand customers, some of whom now believe the robot's days are numbered. The company also released an Astro for businesses in 2023, before sunsetting it less than a year later.
Amazon isn't giving up on Bezos' dream of a household robot just yet, despite its stumbles with Astro.
Over the past several months, the company has assembled a new team that's working on a "new-to-world robot product," according to a CNBC analysis of job posts.
"Robots are about to step out of the movies and into our homes," a recent job listing for an engineer, which has since been removed, stated. The post details a product capable of navigating "dynamic home environments" and "autonomous operation alongside family members."
Amazon is known for making long-term bets at the risk of "being misunderstood" in the short term if it gives the company an early advantage in new markets, like it did with the Alexa voice assistant or Kindle e-reader.
CEO Andy Jassy reminded investors of this approach in his latest annual letter, where he said artificial intelligence and robotics were among the "biggest inflections of our lifetime."
"We try to anticipate what will make customers' lives easier and better every day, and invent the next inflection," Jassy wrote.
Analysts also expect the humanoid market to surge in the coming years. Barclays forecast in a January report that the global market, which it currently values at $2 billion to $3 billion, could reach roughly $40 billion by 2035, or as high as $200 billion "under the most optimistic scenarios."
Earlier this year, Amazon redeployed much of the team behind Astro and brought in an MIT roboticist to work on the home robot project, LinkedIn profiles show.
It also made a splashy acquisition to supercharge the effort.
In March, Amazon scooped up New York-based Fauna Robotics, which has built a 3.5-foot-tall humanoid called Sprout. At the time, the company said Fauna would become part of a new division dubbed the Personal Robotics Group.
Some Personal Robotics Group staffers previously worked in Amazon's Lab126 R&D unit, which has been behind many of Amazon's most successful consumer hardware products, like the Kindle e-reader, Echo smart speakers, Fire TV and Fire Tablet. Lab126 was also behind one of Amazon's biggest flops, the Fire Phone.
It's unclear what kind of home robot the group is developing, or the types of tasks it could handle, but a June job posting hinted at an effort to "create robots that are not just functional, but delightful."
Amazon could be looking to adapt Fauna's robots for homes or businesses. The Sprout humanoid, which was designed to be "friendly and capable" with expressive yellow eyebrows, has primarily been used by developers, as well as commercial and academic researchers.
An Amazon job posting published online in October describes a "Field Support Engineer" who can assist with customer support and on-site repair, while another listing seeks a user experience designer to "define what it feels like to live with a Fauna robot."
"Our goal is simple: make robots people actually want to live and interact with in everyday human spaces," the listing states.
Amazon spokesperson Brad Glasser told CNBC in a statement that the company acquired Fauna because it's "committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category."
"We're optimistic about a future where personal robots are helping people in meaningful ways in everyday life, and we intend to play an important role in making that future a reality," Glasser said.
Glasser noted that there remains a substantial gap between what's possible in a controlled lab and what's possible in settings like the living room or a lobby. Amazon is working with the robotics community to solve these challenges, he said.
Emily Lugo Velez has been living with the Astro in her North Carolina home since 2023. Lugo Velez, who worked in IT and now runs an AI advisory business, said she and her husband weren't fazed by the robot's $1,000-plus price tag and quickly joined the waitlist.
"We spent so much money on this thing," Lugo Velez, 52, said in an interview. "I feel like we're just stuck with it, and we'll let it run around the house until it eventually dies, then send it to the trash heap."
She said she still uses the device to check on her pets and appliances when she's out of the house. But beyond that, Astro has primarily become a party trick and a "trip hazard."
Most days, she tells Astro to go back to its charging dock.
Executives who worked on Astro had discussed making it more capable by attaching an arm to pick up and inspect items without breaking them, said Ken Washington, who served as Amazon's VP of consumer robotics until 2023.
He told CNBC that he pushed for a bipedal robot, but leadership disagreed.
"We had Jeff [Bezos] in for show and tells and reviews, and I watched his body language pretty closely," Washington said. "I think he was disappointed with the lack of functionality, but I think he was impressed with its ability to map and navigate an undefined space under all lighting conditions."
For all the struggles with Astro, Amazon has a rich history in robotics.
The company acquired Kiva Systems for $775 million in 2012, which introduced mobile robots to its vast fulfillment network. Since then, Amazon's warehouse automation efforts have ballooned to over one million robots across its facilities that can pick, sort and ferry items to workers.
But homes offer unique obstacles for robots to navigate.
"The home is a completely different space," said Jeff Burnstein, president of the trade group Association for Advancing Automation, who has been in the robotics industry for 45 years. "Children, pets, grandparents, stairways. Nobody's home is set up exactly the same, so it's a much more challenging environment for a robot, certainly a robot that's walking."
Amazon may have more luck its second time around because the tools for building robots have advanced by "leaps and bounds" over the past few years, said Colin Angle, a co-founder and former CEO of Roomba maker iRobot.
Amazon attempted to acquire iRobot in 2022 before walking away from the deal two years later amid growing regulatory pushback.
"The toolkit that the Astro team had when they did it was clubs with nails in them, just incredibly primitive," Angle said. "It's difficult to understate just how much the robot industry has changed in the last two years."
Advances in AI models, sensors, battery systems and key mechanical components like actuators have spurred a new wave of development around robots for industrial and consumer use.
Elon Musk's Tesla has been developing its bipedal Optimus robots since 2021. Startups including Apptronik, Boston Dynamics, China's Unitree, Figure and 1X are also building humanoids. Agility Robotics, the company behind the bipedal Digit robot that counts Amazon as one of its backers, went public via a SPAC on Thursday.
Venture capital firms poured $33.4 billion into robotics and physical AI companies in the first half of the year, compared with $28.7 billion for all of 2025, according to PitchBook data.
Most humanoids are being developed with the manufacturing, logistics and healthcare industries in mind, but a growing group of companies are attempting to build robots for the home.
Apple is reportedly working on several home robot projects, including a tabletop device that resembles the Pixar lamp. Hugging Face, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for almost $13 billion in September, released the $399 Microduck in August. Angle, in May, launched a startup building fuzzy companion robots called Familiar Machines & Magic. Companies including Sunday, Tau and Nori claim their robots can help with household chores like folding laundry and clearing the table, but they remain mostly prototype or niche devices.
"[Astro] was so ahead of its time," Washington said. "It was such a big, massive leap that I felt like we had the right to own the home."
The robot's limited functionality and its $1,000-plus price tag likely made it a tough sell for many consumers, said a former Amazon employee who worked on Astro, who asked not to be named in order to speak frankly about the project.
"Our poor little Astro was around $2,000 when it came out, and that's a lot," the ex-employee said. "That's a lot for a consumer, and they want a robot that does a lot."
Amazon takes a long term view on new markets like personal robotics, and values what can be gained by being an early entrant, Glasser said.
Astro was designed to help Amazon build competencies and focus its ambition, he added. The company has applied many of the learnings, talent and experience from Astro into its other robotics efforts, Glasser said.
In Facebook groups for Astro owners, users have complained of diminished customer service and griped that Amazon's AIexa+ AI assistant isn't supported on Astro.
Some users have interpreted this to mean Astro could be discontinued. Others have tried to dump their units at a discount on eBay and Facebook Marketplace.
Glasser said Amazon continues to support Astro customers.
Joe Martin, an Astro owner who lives near Tucson, Arizona, said he feels he's gotten his money's worth out of the device over the past four years. He'd welcome another robot into his home if it could do more, like helping out around the house.
"Astro was $1,000 and it was pretty limited, but if it could bring a drink to me or dust furniture, I'd be intrigued by that," Martin, 65, said. "I think that's right around the corner."

articles.title: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
articles.text:
Airline ticket prices have surged this year, especially for travel over the holidays. Don't expect many bargains if you're booking flights with miles, either.
Tickets bought with frequent flyer miles for flights between large U.S. airports over the Thanksgiving travel period will cost 32% more than last year's holiday, according to data from Seats.aero, a miles and points redemption search site. While fares have skyrocketed this year, airline executives last month said demand remains strong.
Airlines have largely gotten rid of static mileage redemption charts in favor of dynamic pricing, making budgeting for an award ticket more difficult. Dynamic pricing means redemption costs change depending on demand, routes and other factors.
Many of the most expensive routes this Thanksgiving are understandably longer, including from Hawaii, but the list also includes a nonstop from New York to Houston.
Here's how mileage redemptions for the holiday are stacking up, based on one-way flights on average as of early November and compared with last year:
Jet fuel prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, which has eaten into airline profits. Carriers have sought to pass costs along to consumers as much as possible.
Even some of the cheapest routes for award tickets are more expensive than last year, including for short routes like Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.
